yaa-asantewaa: Yaa Asantewaa was born around 1840 in Besease, the daughter of Kwaku Ampoma and Ata Po. She farmed land around Boankra and married a man from Kumasi, with whom she had a daughter. Her older brother, the Ejisuhene, or paramount chief of Ejisu, appointed her Queen Mother of Ejisu.

In Ashanti society, which traces descent through women, the post was prestigious: the Queen Mother advised the king, chose candidates for the next king and was responsible for protecting the Golden Stool. When her brother died in 1894 she nominated her own grandson as Ejisuhene. In 1896 the British exiled him to the Seychelles, along with Prempeh I, the King of Asante, and other members of the Asante government, and she became regent of the Ejisu–Juaben district.

After Prempeh's exile the British governor of the Gold Coast, Frederick Hodgson, demanded the Golden Stool, the symbol of the Asante nation. The remaining members of the Asante government met secretly at Kumasi and disagreed over how to win the king's return. Yaa Asantewaa rose and told the chiefs that if they would not fight, they should exchange their loincloths for her undergarments, and she fired a gun in front of the men. A number of regional kings chose her as war leader of the Asante forces, the first and only time a woman held that role in Asante history.

The War of the Golden Stool, also called the Yaa Asantewaa War, began in March 1900 with a siege of the British fort at Kumasi, where the British had taken refuge. After several months the governor sent a force of 1,400 to end the rebellion. Yaa Asantewaa and fifteen of her closest advisers were captured and exiled to the Seychelles.

More than 2,000 Asante warriors and about 1,000 British troops are said to have died. On 1 January 1902 the British annexed Asante as a protectorate. The Golden Stool was never handed over, and a false one is said to have been given to the governor.

She died in exile in the Seychelles on 17 October 1921. On 17 December 1924 Prempeh I and the other exiles were allowed to return, and Prempeh had her remains and theirs brought back for a royal burial. The Asante protectorate gained independence as part of Ghana on 6 March 1957. A song honours her as the woman who fights before cannons. The hundredth anniversary of the war was marked in 2000 by a Yaa Asantewaa festival throughout Ghana, which included the launch of a Yaa Asantewaa Museum.
yaeyama-islands: The Yaeyama Islands are an archipelago in the southwest of Okinawa Prefecture, covering 591.46 square kilometres, southwest of the Miyako Islands. They are the most remote part of Japan from the main islands and include its southernmost inhabited island, Hateruma, and its westernmost, Yonaguni. The city of Ishigaki is the political, cultural and economic centre. Yaeyama Island means multilayered mountains, and the native name Yaima possibly comes from a reconstructed Proto-Ryukyuan form. On maps of the 1700s the group appears under names such as the Majico Sima Group, Nambu Soto and the Taipin Islands. The islands form the southern part of the volcanic Ryukyu chain, and they are divided between Ishigaki City and the districts of Taketomi Town and Yonaguni Town.

The islands support subtropical and tropical plants and mangrove forests, and they produce sugarcane and pineapples. Coral reefs around them shelter dolphins, sea turtles, manta rays and whale sharks. Whales and dugongs were once common, and Yaeyama had the largest dugong population in the Ryukyu Islands before humans wiped them out. On Aragusuku Island a sacred place enshrines hunted dugongs with their skulls, and non-residents may not enter without special permission. The islands are an Important Bird Area. The Yaeyama palm grows only on Ishigaki and Iriomote.

The Yonaguni language is the indigenous language of Yonaguni, and the Yaeyama language that of the other islands, though Japanese is now the main language of most people. The islands produce traditional Okinawan textiles. The Mushaama Festival on Hateruma is a harvest festival held during Obon, with a parade of the local fertility god Miruku and his children, lion dances and staff dances.
yahya-khan: Agha Muhammad Yahya Khan was born on 4 February 1917 in Chakwal, in British India, into a Qizilbash family from Peshawar. He claimed descent from soldiers of the Iranian conqueror Nader Shah. He was commissioned into the British Indian Army in 1939 and served in the 4th Battalion of the 10th Baluch Regiment. In the Second World War he fought in North Africa, where Axis forces captured him in June 1942, and he escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp in Italy at the third attempt.

After partition he joined the Pakistan Army in August 1947, served at the Staff College in Quetta, and at 34 became the youngest brigadier in the army. In 1965 he played a part in Operation Grand Slam, and in September 1966 President Ayub Khan made him commander-in-chief.

A mass movement against Ayub Khan began in West Pakistan in the autumn of 1968 and spread to East Pakistan. In March 1969 Ayub Khan resigned and transferred authority to Yahya, who declared martial law and suspended the constitution. He set a framework for elections and issued the Legal Framework Order in July 1970. In the general elections of 7 December 1970 the Awami League of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman won 160 seats, all in East Pakistan, while Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's Pakistan Peoples Party won 81, all in the west. The electorate was divided along regional lines. Negotiations in Dhaka in March 1971 failed.

On 25 March 1971 Yahya launched Operation Searchlight, a crackdown to suppress the Bengali nationalist movement. The Pakistani government held that it had to put down a rebellion to preserve the country's unity. The operation is widely described as the start of a genocide, and Yahya is regarded as one of its principal architects. Mujibur Rahman declared the independence of Bangladesh. After the surrender of Pakistani forces in the east, public anger spread and rumours of a coup circulated. On 20 December 1971 Yahya handed the presidency to Bhutto.

Bhutto's government placed Yahya under house arrest, first at a forest bungalow near Kharian and from April 1972 at his house in Rawalpindi. The Hamoodur Rahman Commission was set up in December 1971 to investigate the failures in East Pakistan. After a stroke he was released in 1977 by General Fazle Haq, and he died in Rawalpindi on 10 August 1980. He is regarded negatively in Bangladesh as the architect of the genocide, and in Pakistan for failing to prevent the country's division.
yajnavalkya: Yajnavalkya, whose name derives from yajna, 'ritual', is presented as a pupil of Vaisampayana and of Uddālaka Āruṇi, and as the compiler of the Shukla Yajurveda Samhita. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells that Vaisampayana grew angry with him, one of his leading disciples, and demanded back all the knowledge he had taught him. Yajnavalkya vomited it up, and the guru told his other disciples to take the form of partridges, taittiriya birds, and consume it, which gave the Upanishad its name. The story is meant to show his genius, and he is also said to have added his own insight, which pleased the guru. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, dated to about 700 BCE, he is depicted as blunt, provocative and sarcastic.

Yajnavalkya stands at the centre of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. King Janaka of Videha, at Mithila, held a sacrifice called the Bahudakshina Yajna, at which he offered a thousand cows with gold horns to the best brahmin. Yajnavalkya at once told his disciple Samasrava to drive the cows home. When the other sages, led by Asvala, protested, he replied that he did not claim to be the best brahmin, and had simply wanted the cows. A debate followed in which he answered each challenger, among them Uddalaka Aruni, Bhujyu, Sakalya, Artabhaga, Ushasta and Kahola.

The scholar Gargi questioned him twice. In section 3.6 he told her not to question too much, lest her head fall off, when she asked about the support of Brahman. In 3.8 she asked what supports space, and he spoke of the imperishable, the seer who is not seen. She then declared that no other brahmin could defeat him. In chapter 4 he decides to renounce the world and leave his family, and his wife Maitreyi, a discusser of Brahman, asks him about the soul and declines wealth that cannot make her immortal. His other wife, Katyayani, is described as knowing the matters of women.

He is associated with the Shukla Yajurveda, the Shatapatha Brahmana, the two Upanishads and the dharma text Yājñavalkya Smṛti, which sets out conduct, legal procedure and atonement, and was widely known through the commentary Mitakshara by Vijnaneshvara in the mid-twelfth century. The Yoga Yajnavalkya was probably written many centuries later by someone else.

His teaching describes the self by negation, 'not this, not this' (neti neti), and holds that love is love for the self, ātman. It contains one of the earliest expositions of karma and rebirth: a person becomes good by good acts and bad by bad acts. Witzel credits him with coining the term Advaita, and his ideas on renunciation have been important to Hindu sannyasa traditions.
yajurveda: The name Yajurveda joins yajus, meaning a sacrificial prayer or formula, and veda, knowledge. Michael Witzel interprets it as a knowledge text of prose mantras used in Vedic rituals. The text is a compilation of ritual-offering formulas said by a priest while an individual performed ritual actions such as those before the yajña fire. Its core belongs to the classical Mantra period of Vedic Sanskrit. It is younger than the Rigveda and roughly contemporary with the Atharvaveda and the Sāmaveda, and its earliest layer borrows from verses of the Rigveda.

The text is grouped into the black, or Krishna, and the white, or Shukla, Yajurveda. The black label implies an unarranged, motley collection, while the white implies a well-arranged one. In the Krishna Yajurveda each recension mixes its Brahmana commentary into the collection of mantras, while in the Shukla version the two are kept apart.

The earliest layer of the Yajurveda samhita holds about 1,875 verses. The Shukla Yajurveda's collection is called the Vajasaneyi Samhita, after Vajasaneya, the patronymic of Yajnavalkya, and it has forty chapters. Only two of its many recensions survive, the Madhyandina and the Kanva, which are nearly identical. Four recensions of the Krishna Yajurveda survive: the Taittirīya, Maitrayani, Kaṭha and Kapiṣṭhala samhitas. The Maitrayani is the oldest Yajurveda samhita to survive. The mantras are typically set in a metre and call on Vedic deities such as Savita, Indra, Agni, Prajapati and Rudra.

The middle layer includes the Satapatha Brahmana, the Brahmana of the Hundred Paths, one of the largest Brahmana texts. Its youngest layer includes six primary Upanishads: the Brihadaranyaka, Isha, Taittiriya, Katha, Shvetashvatara and Maitri. The Katha Upanishad tells of the boy Nachiketa, who meets Yama, the deity of death, and discusses the nature of the self.

The text is a useful source on agriculture and economic and social life in the Vedic era. A verse of the White Yajurveda lists rice, barley, beans, sesame, millets, wheat and lentils among the crops for which the offerer prays. Two of the oldest surviving manuscripts of Shukla Yajurveda sections, found in Nepal and Western Tibet, are dated to the 12th century CE.

Most surviving manuscripts remain untranslated into Western languages. The two reliable translations are from the colonial period: A. B. Keith's of the Taittiriya Samhita and Eggeling's of the Satapatha Brahmana. In the 18th century French Jesuits published the Ezourvedam, claiming it was a translation of a recension of the Yajurveda, but it was later declared a forgery.
yakov-sverdlov: Sverdlov was born on 3 June 1885 (22 May O.S.) in Nizhny Novgorod to a Jewish family active in revolutionary politics; his father was an engraver who forged documents and stored arms for the underground. After four years of gymnasium he left to become a pharmacist's apprentice, joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1902 and supported Lenin's Bolshevik faction from 1903. He took part in the 1905 revolution in the Urals. From his arrest in June 1906 until 1917 he was mostly imprisoned or exiled, and in 1914-1916 he was in internal exile in Turukhansk, Siberia, along with Joseph Stalin.

After the February Revolution Sverdlov returned to Petrograd, met Lenin in April 1917 and in August was elected one of five members of the Central Committee's Secretariat. He helped plan the October Revolution and the decision to stage an armed uprising. In November 1917 he was elected chairman of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee, the de facto head of state, and in March 1918 chairman of the Secretariat. He played roles in the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly in January 1918 and in the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March. His organizing ability was well regarded, and thousands of local party committees were started during his chairmanship.

Sverdlov supported the Red Terror. After the assassination of Moisei Uritsky and the attempt on Lenin's life in August 1918 he drafted a document calling for merciless mass terror against the enemies of the revolution, and he took over some of Lenin's duties during his recovery. He also backed decossackization, which killed thousands of Cossacks. Many sources claim that he, with Lenin and Filipp Goloshchyokin, played a major part in the execution of Nicholas II and his family on 17 July 1918, and Trotsky's diaries record Sverdlov telling him "We decided it here."

Sverdlov died on 16 March 1919, aged 33, most commonly attributed to the Spanish flu contracted after a visit to Ukraine and Oryol, and was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. Mikhail Kalinin eventually succeeded him as chairman of the Central Executive Committee. Some historians see his early death as a factor in Stalin's rise, since Sverdlov was a natural candidate for the post of General Secretary. Yekaterinburg was renamed Sverdlovsk in 1924 and regained its name in 1991.
yakuts: Scholars have proposed several origins for the Yakuts. In the 19th century Nikolai Schukin, working from local oral histories, introduced the view that Khakas groups from the southern Yenisey migrated north to the Lena, and Nikolai Kozmin gave the most authoritative support to this Yenisey hypothesis in 1928.

Many researchers conclude that the Yakuts arose from Turkic migrants from the Lake Baikal region mixing with the native Yukaghir and Tungusic peoples of the Lena. Yakut tradition remembers earlier peoples such as the Tumats, with whom there was conflict and some intermarriage. According to one account the Yakuts began to move to the basins of the Middle Lena, the Aldan and the Vilyuy from the 13th century, under pressure from the rising Mongols.

In the 1620s the Tsardom of Muscovy moved into Yakut territory, imposed a fur tax called yasak and put down several Yakut rebellions between 1634 and 1642. Brutal collection of the tax provoked a rebellion in 1642 among the Yakuts and the Tungusic-speaking tribes along the Lena. The voivode Peter Golovin answered with a reign of terror in which settlements were burned and hundreds killed. The Yakut population is estimated to have fallen by 70 percent between 1642 and 1682, mainly through smallpox and other infectious diseases.

Gold and then the Trans-Siberian Railway brought more Russians. By the 1820s almost all Yakuts claimed to have converted to the Russian Orthodox church, though they kept a number of tengri practices. Yakut literature began to rise in the late 19th century, and a national revival followed in the early 20th. After the Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1922, collectivisation brought systematic persecution from the late 1920s to the late 1930s, and the Yakut population fell from 240,500 in 1926 to 236,700 in 1959 before recovering.

The Yakuts practise animal husbandry. They have traditionally raised horses, reindeer and a hardy breed of cattle suited to the harsh climate. According to one account, northern Yakuts were largely hunters, fishermen and reindeer herders, while the southern Yakuts raised cattle and horses. Their language, Yakut or Sakha, belongs to the northern branch of the Siberian Turkic languages and is most closely related to Dolgan. Their cuisine includes the fermented mare's-milk drink kumis, dairy products, stroganina, which is sliced frozen salted fish, horse meat and salamat, a millet porridge with butter and horse fat.
yakutsk: Yakutsk lies in the Central Yakutian Lowland, about 450 km south of the Arctic Circle, and is a major port on the Lena River. It is built on continuous permafrost. Its average annual temperature is −8.0 °C, and a record low of −64.4 °C has been recorded.

The land was inhabited long before the Russians arrived: more than 200 archaeological sites have been explored within the city, the oldest, the Yubileinaya site, estimated at 20,500 to 10,000 years old. The Yakuts, also called the Sakha, settled the Tuymaada Valley in the 13th to 16th centuries and mixed with the Evenk and Yukagir peoples.

On 25 September 1632 (5 October in the modern calendar) a detachment under the Yenisei sotnik Pyotr Beketov established the Lensky Ostrog on the right bank of the Lena, 70 km downstream from the present city, on the land of the Borogon Yakuts. It began with a garrison of 30 Cossacks, survived a siege by the Yakuts in 1634, and in 1638 became the centre of the new Yakutsk Voivodeship. In 1642 to 1643 it was moved to its present site in the Tuymaada Valley.

Yakutsk received city status in 1708 and was the military, administrative and commercial centre of the Lena region. It was the starting point for expeditions by Mikhail Stadukhin, Semyon Dezhnev, Vladimir Atlasov, Ivan Moskvitin, Vasily Poyarkov and Yerofey Khabarov. Yakutia became an oblast in 1851. The Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was formed on 27 April 1922, the first statehood of the Yakut people, with Yakutsk as its capital. During the Second World War the city administered the Alsib air route, by which about 8,000 aircraft were delivered from the United States.

Yakutsk is the capital and largest city of the Sakha Republic in Russia, with a population of 355,443 at the 2021 census. It is the largest city on continuous permafrost and the coldest city in the world of over 200,000 people. Its economy grew after the Second World War with the development of the region's mineral resources, and the North-Eastern Federal University was founded there in 2010.
yale-university: Yale traces its beginnings to An Act for Liberty to Erect a Collegiate School, passed in New Haven by the General Court of the Colony of Connecticut on 9 October 1701. The act aimed to establish an institution for the education of ministers and lay leaders. Soon afterwards ten Congregational ministers, all Harvard alumni, met in the study of the Reverend Samuel Russell in Branford and donated books to form the school's library. Led by James Pierpont, they are now known as the Founders.

The Collegiate School was one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the American Revolution. Its curriculum was at first centred on theology and sacred languages, and had expanded to include the humanities and sciences by the time of the Revolution.

The Yale Report of 1828 was a defence of the Latin and Greek curriculum against critics who wanted more modern languages, mathematics and science. It meant the classics would not be abandoned. Later William Graham Sumner, professor from 1872 to 1909, taught economics and sociology to overflowing classrooms and prevailed over President Noah Porter, who objected to Sumner's use of a textbook by Herbert Spencer.

In the 19th century Yale added graduate and professional instruction, awarded the first PhD in the United States in 1864, and organised as a university in 1887. Its faculty and student numbers grew rapidly after 1890 with the expansion of the campus and its scientific research. Milton Winternitz led the School of Medicine as dean from 1920 to 1935 and introduced the Yale System of teaching, with few lectures and fewer examinations.

Yale is governed by the Yale Corporation, which has 19 members, while the faculty of each school oversees its curriculum. Its main campus covers 260 acres in downtown New Haven. The residential college system was established in 1933 by Edward S. Harkness, who admired Oxford and Cambridge. The colleges have heads and academic deans but contain no programmes of study. The Yale Literary Magazine, founded in February 1836, is the oldest student literary magazine in the United States.
yalu-river: The Yalu rises at about 2,500 metres on Paektu Mountain, on the China–North Korea border. It flows south to Hyesan, then sweeps 130 kilometres north-west to Linjiang, and returns to a more southerly course for a further 300 kilometres before emptying into Korea Bay between Dandong in China and Sinuiju in North Korea. Together with the Tumen River to the east and a small portion of Paektu Mountain, it forms the border between the two countries. It is not easily navigable for most of its length, and most of it freezes in winter.

The river basin is where the ancient Korean kingdom of Goguryeo rose to power. Many of its fortresses stand along the river, and its former capital stood at what is now the city of Ji'an, a site rich in Goguryeo-era remains. In 1388, on Wihwa Island in the river, General Yi Songgye, later Taejo of Joseon, decided to turn his army back south towards Kaesong, the first of a series of revolts that led to the founding of the Joseon dynasty. According to one scholar, the border along the Yalu is the longest unchanged international border in history, lasting at least 1,000 years.

Its position between Korea and China made it the scene of several battles, including the Battle of the Yalu River of 1894 in the First Sino-Japanese War and a battle in 1904 in the Russo-Japanese War. During Japanese rule from 1910 to 1945 the southern side was heavily industrialised.

In the Korean War, United Nations troops moved towards the river despite repeated Chinese warnings, which precipitated massive Chinese intervention from around Dandong. Every bridge across the river except the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge between Sinuiju and Dandong was destroyed. The valley at the western end of the river became a focus of air combat over North Korea, nicknamed MiG Alley. The Chinese People's Volunteers Army Song of 1950, which mentions the Yalu, became one of the best-known musical expressions of the intervention.

The river is important for hydroelectric power. The Sup'ung Dam, 106 metres high and over 850 metres long, is one of the largest dams in Asia. About 205 islands lie in the river, and a 1962 border treaty divided them according to which ethnic group lived on each, giving North Korea 127 and China 78. The estuary is an Important Bird Area.
yamagata-aritomo: Yamagata was born in Hagi, the castle town of the Chōshū Domain, to a low-ranking samurai family of the chūgen class. His mother died when he was five and his grandmother Katsu raised him. In 1858 he went to Kyoto as an intelligence agent for the domain, on the recommendation of Yoshida Shōin, and then studied under Yoshida at the Shōka Sonjuku. Wounded in the bombardment of Shimonoseki in 1864, he became convinced of the superiority of Western military technology. He served in the Kiheitai, a militia of men from all social classes, and led Chōshū forces in the Boshin War of 1868.

From 1869 to 1870 Yamagata toured Europe with Saigō Tsugumichi to study military systems, and he was impressed by Prussian universal conscription. He was the primary driver behind the Conscription Act, which made military service compulsory for all male citizens regardless of class. Peasants resented it as a blood tax and some samurai opposed it. As field commander he crushed the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, led by Saigō Takamori. In 1878 he set up an independent Imperial Army General Staff on the Prussian model, reporting directly to the emperor, which separated military command from civilian government.

Yamagata became Home Minister in 1883 and centralised local government and the police. As prime minister from December 1889 he oversaw the opening of the first Imperial Diet in 1890, and in a speech that March he described a line of sovereignty and a line of interest, which he identified with Korea. After the First Sino-Japanese War, in which he commanded the First Army until illness cut short his command, he pressed to double the army from seven to thirteen divisions. His second cabinet began in November 1898; in 1899 civil service ordinances made it harder for party members to hold high bureaucratic posts, and in May 1900 only active-duty generals and admirals could serve as army and navy ministers. He resigned in October 1900.

After 1900 Yamagata was a genrō and rival of Itō Hirobumi, and during the Russo-Japanese War he was the final authority on military strategy as Chief of the Army General Staff. In 1920-1921 he tried to block the marriage of Crown Prince Hirohito, citing hereditary colour blindness in the bride's family; he failed, to the harm of his prestige. He died on 1 February 1922 at his villa in Odawara and was given a state funeral. His legacy is contested: in the West and postwar Japan he is often depicted as the arch-villain of Japanese militarism, while others see a cautious and pragmatic statesman concerned with national security.
yamagata-prefecture: Yamagata Prefecture lies in the south-western corner of Tōhoku, facing the Sea of Japan, and covers 9,325 km2. It borders Akita Prefecture to the north, Miyagi Prefecture to the east, and Fukushima and Niigata prefectures to the south. Mountain ranges mark all these boundaries, and most of the population lives in a limited central plain. Yamagata, the capital and largest city, is joined among the major cities by Tsuruoka, Sakata and Yonezawa.

The climate has long, hot, humid summers and long, snowy winters, with short and rather dry springs and autumns. The central mountains around Gassan may see as much as 3,000 centimetres of snow in a season, while the coast at Sakata is milder. The prefecture is the largest producer of cherries and pears in Japan.

The Ezo people were the aboriginal inhabitants of the area. Together with what is now Akita Prefecture it formed Dewa Province until the Meiji Restoration. During the Heian period (794–1185) the Fujiwara family ruled the region. Yamagata city flourished in the Edo period (1603–1867) as a castle town and post station, known for beni, the red safflower dye used for handspun silk. In 1689 the haiku poet Matsuo Bashō visited Yamagata on his five-month journey through the northern regions.

The area has long been a centre of religious practice. The Dewa Sanzan, three holy mountains, form a traditional pilgrimage for followers of Shugendō, a branch of Shinto, and the five-storey pagoda at the base of Mount Haguro, the lowest of the three, is a National Treasure. The temple of Yama-dera is carved into the mountainside near Yamagata city. Ginzan Onsen, a hot-spring town in the mountains of Obanazawa, originally grew up around a silver mine.

Yamagata is known for its Hanagasa Festival, held in the city on the first weekend in August, and for a snow lantern festival at the Uesugi Shrine in Yonezawa. Starting in 2003 a project catalogued the Buddhist art of 190 temples in Yamagata city and found a rare seated Vairocana Buddha of zelkova wood at Heisenji Temple, as well as sculpture of the Heian and Kamakura periods. Seventeen per cent of the land is designated as Natural Parks, and Mount Zaō is known for its ski slopes and the Okama crater lake.
yamaguchi-city: Yamaguchi lies almost in the centre of Yamaguchi Prefecture. Its area is the largest in the prefecture and runs long from north to south, facing the Seto Inland Sea (Yamaguchi Bay) at its southern end and bordering Shimane Prefecture in the north. The Fushino River runs through the middle of the Yamaguchi Basin, and the urban areas lie on both sides of it. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot summers and cool winters, and rain is heaviest in summer.

The area was part of the ancient Suō Province. In the Muromachi period it was ruled by the Ōuchi clan, who at their height held six provinces in the Chūgoku region of western Japan. The Ōuchi claimed descent from the royal house of Baekje and grew wealthy through extensive trade with Korea and Ming China. After the Ōnin War they welcomed intellectuals who had escaped from Kyoto, and Yamaguchi prospered as a centre of culture.

Later in the Muromachi period Christian missionaries from Spain and Portugal were welcomed, and the area became an early centre of the Kirishitan faith. The Ōuchi were eventually overthrown by their vassals, the Mōri clan, who ruled the area as part of Chōshū Domain in the Edo period.

After the Meiji Restoration the town of Yamaguchi was established on 1 April 1889. It became a city on 10 April 1929, when the town absorbed the village of Yoshiki, and later grew by merging with neighbouring towns and villages, among them Ogōri, Ajisu, Tokuji and Aio in 2005 and Atō in 2010.

Yamaguchi is the capital of Yamaguchi Prefecture, with 193,966 inhabitants at the 2020 census. Its economy rests mainly on commerce, tourism, distribution and public facilities, and it has a small industrial base. It is the seat of Yamaguchi University and other colleges. Among its sights are Rurikō-ji, a Buddhist temple with a five-story pagoda that is a national treasure, the garden of Jōei-ji, a National Historic Site, the castle ruins of Kōnomine and the Ōuchi-shi Yakata, and the Yamaguchi Xavier Memorial Church. The poet Chuya Nakahara and the prime ministers Terauchi Masatake and Kishi Nobusuke came from the city.
yamaguchi-prefecture: Yamaguchi Prefecture lies in the Chūgoku region at the western tip of Honshu. It has coasts on the Sea of Japan and the Seto Inland Sea, and the Kanmon Straits separate it from the island of Kyushu. It covers 6,112 km2 and borders Shimane Prefecture to the north and Hiroshima Prefecture to the northeast. Besides Yamaguchi and Shimonoseki, the major cities include Ube, Shūnan and Iwakuni. Its position on the straits has made it a link to northern Kyushu, and it has long been tied to the Kanmon Straits metropolitan area.

The prefecture was created by the merger of the provinces of Suō and Nagato. During the rise of the samurai in the Heian and Kamakura periods, the Ouchi family of Suō and the Koto family of Nagato became powerful warrior clans. In the Muromachi period Ouchi Hiroyo, the 24th ruler of the Ouchi, conquered both provinces. The Ouchi modelled their city on Kyoto and grew wealthy from cultural imports from the continent and trade with Korea and Ming China, so that Yamaguchi came to be called the Kyoto of the West.

Sue Harutaka defeated the 31st Ouchi ruler, and the Sue were in turn defeated by Mōri Motonari, whose family came to control the Chūgoku region. After Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated Mōri Terumoto at Sekigahara in 1600, Terumoto was forced to give up all his land except Suō and Nagato, where he built his castle at Hagi. The Mōri promoted salt, rice and paper in a campaign known as the Three Whites.

After Commodore Matthew Perry opened Japan, clans from Nagato, also called Chōshū, played a key part in the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate and the setting up of the new imperial government. Shipbuilding, chemical, machinery and metalworking plants were built in the harbours of the Seto Inland Sea in the Taishō period (1912–1926), and after World War II petrochemical complexes made it one of the most industrialised prefectures in Japan.

The prefecture had a population of 1,377,631 in 2018, and its population has fallen in most years since 1985. Politicians from Yamaguchi, drawing on the Chōshū role in the Meiji Restoration, have held many high offices; the Kishi, Satō and Abe family forms the best-known prime ministerial line of the post-war era. Visitors go to the five-arched wooden Kintai Bridge at Iwakuni, the Akiyoshido cave, said to be Japan's longest, and Hagi, whose reverberatory furnace is a World Heritage Site.
yamamoto-tsunetomo: Yamamoto Tsunetomo was born on 11 June 1659 to Yamamoto Jin'emon, then aged 71, and a woman whose maiden name was Maeda. He was the last child of the family, and his father regarded him as a superfluous addition who was to be given away to a salt merchant. For most of his childhood Tsunetomo was sickly, and he later claimed that doctors had told him he would not live past twenty. At the age of nine he was nonetheless employed as a page to Nabeshima Mitsushige, whose interest in his literary skill led him to have the boy study under the man of letters Kuranaga Rihei.

In his twenties Tsunetomo studied under the Zen Buddhist priest Tannen and the Confucian scholar Ishida Ittei, both of whom greatly influenced his thinking. His older nephew Yamamoto Gorōzaemon helped him obtain a post as a scribe in Edo and then, in 1686, in Kyoto. In 1687 Gorōzaemon took responsibility for a destructive fire, and both men resigned. Tsunetomo then returned to Mitsushige's service.

In 1695 Mitsushige retired because of ill health and asked Tsunetomo to find a copy of the Kokindenju, a book of secret instruction in poetry. Tsunetomo presented one to his lord on 1 May 1700, and Mitsushige died two weeks later. Tsunetomo meant to kill himself in order to follow his master in death, but both Mitsushige and the shogunate had banned the practice. Instead he became a Buddhist priest, and his wife became a nun. They lived in a hermitage in the mountains.

Between 1709 and 1716 Tsunetomo narrated many of his thoughts to the samurai Tashiro Tsuramoto. Many of the aphorisms concerned Mitsushige's father and grandfather and the failing ways of the samurai caste. They were compiled and published in 1716 as the Hagakure, a title that can be translated as In the Shadow of Leaves or Hidden Leaves.

Tsunetomo held that becoming one with death in thought, even in life, was the highest attainment of purity and focus. He criticised the carefully planned vendetta of the Forty-seven rōnin of Akō for its delay. The work was little known after his death in 1719, but by the 1930s it had become one of the best-known representatives of bushido taught in Japan, and in the militarist years soldiers hailed it as a key text for proper samurai behaviour.
yamuna: The Yamuna rises in the Yamunotri Glacier on the south-western slopes of the Bandarpunch peaks of the Lower Himalaya in Uttarakhand. It enters Himachal Pradesh and then flows into the Indo-Gangetic plains of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh, passing Delhi, and drains an area of 366,223 square kilometres, 40.2 per cent of the Ganges Basin. It meets the Ganges at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj, a site of the Kumbh Mela, which is held every 12 years. Its tributaries include the Tons, its largest, the Chambal, the Sindh, the Betwa and the Ken. With the Ganges it forms the fertile Ganges–Yamuna Doab.

The earliest mention of the Yamuna is in the Rig Veda, composed in the Vedic period, and it also appears in the Atharvaveda and in Brahmanas such as the Aitareya and Shatapatha. Greek sources know it as Iomanes, in the surveys of Seleucus I Nicator, who visited India in 305 BCE. In the Mahabharata the Pandava capital of Indraprastha stood on its banks, at the site of modern Delhi.

The river's waters have long been used for irrigation. Some canals date to the Tughlaq dynasty in the 14th century, which built the Nahr-i-Bahisht, or Paradise canal, parallel to the river. The Mughals restored and extended it in the first half of the 17th century under the engineer Ali Mardan Khan, to near the capital Shahjahanabad, the present Delhi.

In Hinduism the river is venerated as the goddess Yamuna, daughter of the sun god Surya and his wife Saranyu and twin sister of Yama, the god of death. According to tradition, bathing in her waters frees one from the torments of death, and the Padma Purana says they cleanse the mind of sin. The Rig Veda counts the Yamuna among the seven sacred rivers, and in Gupta art she and the Ganges appear on temple doorjambs to purify those who pass through.

The Yamunotri temple, dedicated to the goddess near the river's source, is among the holiest shrines of Hinduism. The river is closely associated with Krishna: the Puranas tell how he subdued the Naga Kaliya, who had terrorised the people of Braja, and the river is a centre of pilgrimage for his devotees.
yamunanagar-district: Yamunanagar district lies at the north-eastern tip of Haryana and covers 1,756 square kilometres. It is bounded by Himachal Pradesh to the north, Uttar Pradesh to the east, Karnal district to the south, Kurukshetra district to the south-west and Ambala district to the west. The land is plain, with the Siwalik hills on the northern side. Its hilly part, Kalesar, borders the Sirmaur district of Himachal Pradesh and contains Kalesar National Park. Monsoon rainfall averages 892 millimetres, much higher than the state average of 462.

The district came into existence on 1 November 1989, and the town of Yamunanagar is its headquarters. Within its bounds stands Lohgarh Fort, the capital of the First Sikh Empire under Baba Banda Singh Bahudur, and the towns of Sadhaura and Mustafabad, the scene of his first victories, also lie in the district.

The district has three sub-divisions, Jagadhri, Radaur and Bilaspur, and four tehsils. The main towns are Bilaspur, Chhachhrauli, Radaur, Jagadhri and Yamunanagar, a municipal corporation; Jagadhri lies next to Yamunanagar and is the older of the twin cities. At the census of 2011 the district had a population of 1,214,205, and 38.94 per cent of the people lived in urban areas. Hindi was the first language of 88.28 per cent, Punjabi of 7.24 per cent, Haryanvi of 1.75 per cent and Urdu of 1.20 per cent.
yanam: Yanam lies in the delta of the Godavari River, at the confluence of the Koringa River, nine kilometres from the Bay of Bengal on the Circar coast. The town is entirely surrounded by Andhra Pradesh. The Bank Canal, which begins at the Dowleswaram headworks of Sir Arthur Cotton's barrage on the Godavari, brings irrigation and drinking water; it is popularly called the French Channel because it was built under a 1949 agreement between the French government and the government of India.

The French established a trading post at Yanaon in 1723, the third French colony in India, but gave it up in 1727 after commercial operations proved unsuccessful. Governor-General Dupleix seized it again in 1731, and the Nizam of Hyderabad confirmed the French hold in 1751. Until the end of the Napoleonic wars Yanam passed intermittently under British control, and it was finally restored to France in 1814. Its Tuesday market drew Telugu people of the Madras Presidency, who came to buy foreign and smuggled goods.

On 13 June 1954 a coup in Yanam joined it to the Republic of India. The de facto transfer of the four enclaves of Pondicherry, Yanam, Mahé and Karikal took place on 1 November 1954. A treaty of cession was signed on 28 May 1956, but the legal transfer waited until the end of the Algerian War: the French parliament ratified the treaty in May 1962, and on 16 August 1962 the instruments of ratification were exchanged. The enclaves became the Union Territory of Pondicherry on 7 January 1963. After the liberation about 10,000 people in Yanam chose French nationality.

Yanam is a district of the Union Territory of Puducherry. The 1956 treaty kept the former colonies' special administrative status, and French remains an official language of the territory alongside Telugu and English. The town blends French and Telugu culture, which gave it the nickname Frelugu. Its population was 31,362 at the census of 2001. Among its monuments is the Vishnalayam, a 15th-century temple to Venkateswara.
yanan: Yan'an is a prefecture-level city in the Shaanbei region of Shaanxi province, on the Loess Plateau. It borders Shanxi to the east across the Yellow River and Gansu to the west across the Ziwu Ridge. The land is hilly, ranging from 388.8 to 1,809.8 metres above sea level, and the Yellow River, the Yan River and the Luo River flow through it. Yaodong, cave dwellings cut into the hillsides, are traditional homes of northern Shaanxi.

The area was populated at least as early as the Xia dynasty. After the Qin dynasty was established in 221 BCE it formed part of Shang Commandery, and the Sui dynasty organized it as Yan'an Commandery with a military base. Under the Song it was a border fortress against the Tangut-led Western Xia, and in 1080 the polymath Shen Kuo was sent to Yan Prefecture to aid its defence; in autumn 1081 he defended Song territory and captured several nearby fortified towns. In 1221 combined Mongol and Western Xia forces defeated a Jin army of 30,000 in the east of the present-day area.
Before the Dungan Revolt of 1862-1877 much of rural Yan'an was inhabited by Chinese Muslims, many of whom were killed or forced to move; Bao'an had 51,000 people in 1823 but only 170 in 1868.

In October 1935, after the Long March, the Chinese Red Army arrived in the area from Jiangxi. In January 1937 it entered Yan'an without a fight, after local warlords handed the town over, and on 6 September 1937 Yan'an became the seat of the communist government of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region. Thousands of intellectuals travelled there, party members and troops were trained, and in 1941 Mao Zedong launched training programmes that began the Yan'an Rectification Movement.

Japanese bombing destroyed almost every building except a pagoda, and most inhabitants lived in yaodongs. From 1944 to 1947 the United States Army Observation Group, the Dixie Mission, was stationed there. Kuomintang forces briefly captured the city in the Chinese Civil War, after the Communist leadership learned of the attack and withdrew; the People's Liberation Army retook it on 21 April 1948.

Yan'an is regarded by Chinese communists as the birthplace of the revolution, and the Yan'an Revolution Memorial Hall draws visitors who come to learn the party's history. Yan'an University is based in the city. Oil has been extracted from the Changqing Oil Field, part of the Ordos basin, since the early 1970s.
yang-di-pertuan-agong: The title Yang di-Pertuan Agong means He who is made Lord. The office was established in 1957, when the Federation of Malaya gained independence from the United Kingdom. On 31 August 1957 the Conference of Rulers rejected the suggested title Yang di-Pertuan Besar in favour of Yang di-Pertuan Agong and elected the first occupant. By seniority the first in line was the 84-year-old Sultan Ibrahim of Johor, who declined because of age.

The next, the Sultan of Pahang, Abu Bakar, was rejected five times by his fellow electors, in part because his various marriages to celebrities and cabaret dancers were seen as unbecoming. Tuanku Abdul Rahman of Negeri Sembilan, who had been elected to his state throne in 1933, was chosen by eight votes to one.

The Yang di-Pertuan Agong is the constitutional monarch and ceremonial head of state, and the Federal Constitution and Acts of Parliament define his powers. The Constitution vests the federal executive power in him, but with few exceptions he must act on the advice of the Cabinet, and the day-to-day work of government is done by the Cabinet. His discretionary powers concern chiefly the appointment of the prime minister, withholding consent to a dissolution of Parliament and calling meetings of the Conference of Rulers on the privileges and dignities of the rulers. Under the Westminster system he appoints a prime minister who commands the confidence of a majority of the Dewan Rakyat.

He also appoints senior judges, the governors of Penang, Malacca, Sabah and Sarawak and 44 senators, is Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces under Article 41, and is Head of Islam in his own state, the governed states and the federal territories.

The king is elected by secret ballot to a five-year term by and from the nine rulers of the Malay states, who form the Conference of Rulers; the four governors attend but cannot vote. A nominee needs five votes. A ruler who has served may not stand again until all the others have served. Minors are disqualified, and the Conference may declare a ruler unsuitable by a secret ballot of at least five. The office rotates in practice, following the order set by the first cycle of nine kings, 1957 to 1994, which began with the ruler of Negeri Sembilan.

Because it is elective there is no line of succession. In 1993 constitutional amendments removed the legal immunity of the king and the state rulers in their personal capacity, and a Special Court was established to hear proceedings against a ruler.
yangon: Yangon stands in Lower Burma where the Yangon and Bago Rivers meet, about 30 km from the Gulf of Martaban, on the delta of the Irrawaddy. The name comes from the Burmese words yan, meaning enemies, and koun, meaning run out of, and is usually translated as End of Strife. The English form Rangoon is based on the Rakhine dialect. In 1989 the military government changed the city's English name to Yangon, along with many other transliterations; many Burmese did not accept the changes, and neither did a number of publications and foreign governments.

The settlement was founded as Dagon by the Mon people, who then inhabited Lower Burma, in the early 11th century (c. 1028-1043). From the 14th century, under the Hanthawaddy kingdom, it became an important pilgrimage town around its pagoda. Princess Maha Dewi governed it from 1364 to 1392, and her grandniece Shin Saw Pu, later the only female queen regnant in Burmese history, built a palace beside the Shwedagon Pagoda in 1460 and lived there until her death in 1471.

The British captured Yangon and all of Lower Burma in the Second Anglo-Burmese War of 1852 and made the city the commercial and political centre of British Burma, moving the capital there from Moulmein. On a design by the army engineer Lt. Alexander Fraser, they laid out a new city on a grid plan on delta land, bounded on the east by the Pazundaung Creek and on the south and west by the Yangon River. After the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885 it became the capital of all British-ruled Burma. By the 1890s prosperous suburbs had grown north of Royal Lake (Kandawgyi) and Inya Lake, and the British had founded hospitals and colleges, among them Rangoon General Hospital and Rangoon University.

After independence in 1948 many colonial names of streets and parks were replaced by Burmese ones. The city's area grew from 72.52 square kilometres in 1901 to 208.51 in 1974 and 598.75 in 2008, as it spread north towards the airport.

Yangon is the capital of the Yangon Region and the largest city of Myanmar, with about 5.16 million people at the 2014 census, and its main commercial centre. It was the national capital until the government moved its administration to the purpose-built Naypyidaw in 2005-2006. Its colonial-era core, centred on the Sule Pagoda, holds the largest number of colonial-period buildings in Southeast Asia, among them the former High Court, the former Secretariat and the Strand Hotel. The gilded Shwedagon Pagoda is the most sacred Buddhist pagoda of Myanmar. The main religions practised in the city are Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism.
yangtze-river: The Yangtze, called Chang Jiang, or Long River, in Chinese, rises in the Tanggula Mountains of the Tibetan Plateau and flows for 6,300 kilometres in a generally easterly direction to the East China Sea. Its drainage basin comprises one-fifth of the land area of China. The source the Chinese government has traditionally recognised is the Tuotuo tributary at the base of a glacier on Geladandong Mountain, while the hydrologically longest source, at Jari Hill, was discovered only in the late 20th century. The river has over 700 tributaries, among them the Min, Jialing, Han and Gan, and it passes Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing on its way to Shanghai.

Unlike the Yellow River, whose mouth has shifted north and south of the Shandong peninsula, the Yangtze has remained largely static. Human activity is verified in the Three Gorges area as far back as 27,000 years ago. By the 5th millennium BCE the lower Yangtze was a major population centre of the Hemudu and Majiabang cultures, among the earliest cultivators of rice, followed in the 3rd millennium BCE by the Liangzhu culture. What is thought of as Chinese culture developed along the Yellow River, and the Yue of the lower Yangtze, who tattooed their bodies and cut their hair short, were considered barbarous by northerners.

Steamers came late to the upper river between Yichang and Chongqing, where the Three Gorges posed hazards of crosscurrents and whirlpools, and junks were pulled upriver by 70 to 80 trackers. The river was a major barrier between northern and southern China, and until 1957 there was no bridge across it from Yibin to Shanghai. The Central China floods of 1931 were among the deadliest natural disasters ever recorded.

The Yangtze basin is home to nearly one-third of China's population, and the river is the longest in Asia and the largest entirely within a single country. Tens of millions of people live in its floodplain, which floods naturally every summer and is habitable because dikes protect it. The Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric power station in the world by installed capacity. The basin has 416 known fish species, 178 of them found only there, and the Yangtze river dolphin, or baiji, was declared functionally extinct in 2006.
yangzhou: Yangzhou is a prefecture-level city in central Jiangsu Province, on the north bank of the Yangtze. It borders the provincial capital Nanjing to the south-west, Huai'an to the north, Yancheng to the north-east and Taizhou to the east, and Zhenjiang lies across the river. It stands on a plain with many streams and lakes, and the Grand Canal crosses the prefecture from north to south. The name means Rising Prefecture and refers to its former position as the capital of the ancient Yangzhou prefecture. The climate is subtropical monsoon, with winters of about four months.

In the Spring and Autumn period Fuchai, the hegemon of Wu, built the Han Canal to improve supply lines from the region of present-day Suzhou to the North China Plain, where he was fighting Qi. By 486 BCE the canal joined the Yangtze at present-day Yangzhou to the Huai River at present-day Huai'an. The next year Fuchai founded a fortress, Hancheng, to guard its southern end. It was a square of 3 li by 3 li raised about 12 metres above the water on the Yangtze's northern bank, with the canal forming a moat on two sides.

Under the Eastern Han the area formed the Guangling Commandery of Xu Province, whose seat, also called Guangling, lay near the meeting of the Yangtze and the Han Canal. Historically Yangzhou was one of the wealthiest cities in China, known at various periods for its great merchant families, poets, artists and scholars. From the Taiping Rebellion in 1853 to the 1980s it declined through war damage, the neglect of the Grand Canal as railways replaced it, and stagnation. It endured eight years of Japanese occupation in the Second Sino-Japanese War, and in 1943 about 1,200 Allied civilians from Shanghai were interned there.

Yangzhou had a population of 4,559,797 at the 2020 census. The Runyang Yangtze River Bridge carries the road to Zhenjiang, and the harbour at the junction of the Grand Canal and the Yangtze handles passengers and freight for northern Jiangsu, eastern Anhui and south-east Shandong. Yangzhou Railway Station opened in 2004.
yanji: Yanji lies in the east of Jilin Province, among foothills. The main urban area occupies a small, very flat area ringed by mountains dotted with remote farming communities. It lies between 42°50' and 43°23' north and between 129°01' and 129°48' east. The climate is humid continental with long, very cold winters and short, warm, humid summers; the average temperature ranges from about −13 °C in January to about 21.7 °C in August, and most of the annual rainfall of 531 mm falls in summer.

In the 1800s the Qing rulers of China encouraged migration into the area from China proper as part of the Chuang Guandong policy, which aimed to populate Manchuria and stem Russian expansion. From 1934 to 1943 the city was the seat of Jiandao Province in the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo. In 1943 it was renamed Jiandao and made part of the Dongman Consolidated Province.

After the Second World War the city, again called Yanji, was nominally part of a new Songjiang Province. With the communist seizure of power in 1949 the province's borders were changed and Yanji became part of Jilin Province. Yanbian University was founded there in 1949. The railway station was built in 1924. The Korean population grew to become the largest of any Chinese city: the 1990 census placed the ethnic Korean population at over 170,000.

Yanji is a county-level city and the seat of the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture, which lies in eastern Jilin. It is the political, economic and cultural centre of the prefecture, with a population of about 400,000, of which a significant part is ethnic Korean. Both Chinese and Korean are official languages, and official signs are bilingual. The city is a hub of transport and trade between China and North Korea, and in 2009 the Changchun-Yanji Expressway opened.

Yanbian University, the Yanbian University of Science and Technology and the Yanbian Medical College are in the city. An annual Korean folk festival takes place each September, and the North China Travel Fair has been held there every year since 1996.
yankee-doodle: Yankee Doodle is a traditional song and nursery rhyme whose early versions predate the Seven Years' War and the American Revolutionary War. Rumour holds that its earliest words came from a Middle Dutch harvest song on the same tune, supposedly dating to 15th-century Holland.

The word doodle first appeared in English in the early 17th century and is thought to derive from the Low German dudel, meaning playing music badly, or Dödel, meaning fool. In British conversation, Yankee doodle dandy implied an unsophisticated imitation of upper-class fashion, and the fashion historian Peter McNeil claims that the British were insinuating that the colonists were lower-class and lacked masculinity.

According to the usual account, the song was sung by British officers to mock the colonial soldiers who served with them in the French and Indian War. It is said to have been written at Fort Crailo around 1755 or 1758 by the British Army surgeon Richard Shuckburgh, perhaps after seeing the troops of Colonel Thomas Fitch. The date of the earliest known version is disputed. Its first verse tells of Brother Ephraim, who sold his cow, bought a commission and proved a coward in Canada. The tune also appeared in 1762 in The Disappointment, a comic ballad opera from Pennsylvania.

American troops embraced the song and added verses mocking the British and hailing George Washington, and by 1781 it had become a song of national pride. After the Battle of Lexington and Concord, a Boston newspaper reported a British officer saying that the Minutemen had made them dance to the tune until they were tired. The song was played at the British surrender at Saratoga in 1777. According to the Online Etymology Dictionary, the current version seems to have been written in 1776 by Edward Bangs, a Harvard sophomore and Minuteman.

The full version describes a boy who goes with his father to camp, sees Captain Washington on a stallion and flees home to his mother's chamber. It served as one of the de facto national anthems of the United States, with Hail, Columbia and My Country, 'Tis of Thee, until The Star-Spangled Banner was adopted on 3 March 1931, and it is the state song of Connecticut. Its tune is shared by the nursery rhymes Simple Simon, Jack and Jill and Lucy Locket, and by the Japanese dōyō Alps Ichiman Jaku.
yaounde: Yaoundé lies in the Centre Region of Cameroon at an elevation of about 750 metres, between the Nyong and Sanaga rivers at the northern edge of the area's forests. It is thermally equatorial, with a narrow range of temperatures through the year, and has a long wet season from March to November with a lull in July. Two trans-African highways pass through it, and railway lines run west to the port of Douala and north to N'Gaoundéré.

The outpost of Epsumb, or Jeundo, was founded by the German explorers Lt. Richard Kund and Hans Tappenbeck, with the agreement of the chiefs of Ela Esono. From December 1889 to May 1895 the German botanist Georg August Zenker occupied it as an agricultural research station, which he named Jaunde after the local Yaunde or Ewondo people. It served as a base for the rubber and ivory trade, buying from local people in exchange for imported clothing and iron.

In 1895 Major Dominik set up a military garrison at the site, which made possible a Pallotine mission and religious school at nearby Mvolyé. During the First World War Jaunde was occupied by Belgian troops from the Congo. After Germany's defeat France held eastern Cameroon as a mandate of the League of Nations, and Yaoundé was chosen as the capital of the colony in 1922. Douala long remained the more important settlement, but Yaoundé grew rapidly after 1958, because of the cocoa crisis and unrest along the coast, and it has been the seat of government of the Republic of Cameroon since independence.

Yaoundé has more than 2.8 million inhabitants and is the second-largest city in Cameroon after Douala. Its economy is centred on the civil service and the diplomatic services, with tobacco, dairy products, beer, clay, glass goods and timber among its industries. Its landmarks include the Presidential Palace in the Etoudi district, the Palais des Congrès and the Reunification Monument. Cameroon is bilingual, with English and French both official, and the city has schools in both systems.
yaqub-al-mansur: Abu Yusuf Yaqub ibn Yusuf ibn Abd al-Muʾmin al-Mansur was the third Almohad caliph, known also as Moulay Yacoub. His father was Abu Yaqub Yusuf, and his mother was a Christian concubine called Sahir. The historian Rom Landau, a specialist in Arabic, describes his mother as a Negro slave. He later acquired the name Yaqub the Victorious. He succeeded his father in 1184 and died on 23 January 1199.

His father was killed in Portugal on 29 July 1184, and al-Mansur, on reaching Seville with the body on 10 August, was proclaimed caliph at once. He vowed revenge, but fighting against the Banu Ghaniya delayed him in Africa. In 1190 his siege of Tomar, centre of the Portuguese Templars, failed. In 1191 he recaptured Paderne Castle and its territory near Albufeira in the Algarve, held by the Portuguese army of King Sancho I since 1182, and returned to the Maghreb with three thousand Christian captives. The Christians then retook cities including Silves, Vera and Beja, and he came back to defeat them again.

On 18 July 1195 he defeated the army of Castilian King Alfonso VIII at the Battle of Alarcos. It was said that his forces killed 150,000 and took spoils beyond calculation, and after this victory he took the title al-Mansur Billah, Made Victorious by God. He built a monumental gate at the Kasbah of the Udayas in Rabat and a royal citadel and palace complex in Marrakesh, with the Kasbah Mosque and the gate of Bab Agnaou. In Rabat he began a still larger fortified capital and attempted to build what would have been the world's largest mosque.

He was religiously learned, favoured the Zahirite school of jurisprudence in line with Almohad doctrine, and wrote his own book on the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad. He protected the philosopher Averroes. On inheriting the throne he ordered the chief judge Ibn Maḍāʾ to carry out the burning of non-Zahirite religious books, which Ibn Maḍāʾ and his father had banned. The Bimaristan of Marrakesh, the first hospital in Morocco, is counted among his works.

He died in Marrakesh and was buried temporarily in his palace before being taken to Tinmal, where earlier Almohad caliphs and Ibn Tumart were buried. Work on the Rabat mosque and citadel stopped after his death, leaving a large part of the minaret now known as the Hassan Tower. The victory at Alarcos was remembered for centuries and is recounted by Ibn Abi Zar in his Rawd al-Qirtas of 1326.
yaqut-al-hamawi: Yaqut, meaning ruby or hyacinth, was the kunya of Ibn Abdullah, "son of Abdullah". He was born in Constantinople, the Byzantine capital called al-Rum in Arabic, whence his nisba al-Rumi. Captured in war and enslaved, he became the mawali of Askar ibn Abi Nasr al-Hamawi, a trader of Baghdad, from whom he received the laqab al-Hamawi. As Askar's apprentice he learned accounting and commerce and travelled as his envoy, twice or three times, to Kish in the Persian Gulf. In 1194 Askar stopped his salary over some dispute, and Yaqut worked as a copyist and studied under the grammarian al-Ukbari. Five years later he made another mission to Kish for Askar.

On his return to Baghdad Yaqut set up as a bookseller and began to write. He then spent ten years travelling in Iran, Syria and Egypt. His importance as a scholar lies in his testimony to the great, largely lost literary heritage held in libraries east of the Caspian Sea, since he was one of the last visitors before the Mongol invaders destroyed them. He gained much material from the libraries of Merv, where he had studied for two years, and of Balkh. About 1222 he was working on his Geography in Mosul and he completed the first draft in 1224. In 1227 he was in Alexandria, and he moved from there to Aleppo, where he died in 1229.

The Mu'jam al-Buldan, "Dictionary of Countries", was composed between 1224 and 1228 and completed a year before his death. It is classed as a literary geography: an alphabetical index of place names from the literary corpus of the Arabs, with their vocalisations, their Arabic or foreign derivation and their location. Yaqut supplements the geographic descriptions with historical and ethnographic material, accounts of Muslim conquests, names of governors, monuments and local celebrities, and so preserves much early literary, historical, biographical and geographic material, in prose and poetry.

His Mu'jam al-Udaba, the "Literary Encyclopedia" of 1226, is also known as the Irshad al-Arib. Another work, al-Mushtarak, is a lexicon of geographical homonyms, edited by Ferdinand Wüstenfeld in 1846. Wüstenfeld also edited the Mu'jam al-Buldan in six volumes, published at Leipzig.
yarkand: Yarkand, or Yarkant County, lies on the southern rim of the Taklamakan Desert in the Tarim Basin, at an altitude of 1,189 metres, and is administered under Kashgar Prefecture. The oasis is fed by the Yarkand River, which flows north from the Karakorum and through the Kunlun Mountains. It now covers 3,210 square kilometres but was probably far more extensive before a period of desiccation that began from the 3rd century CE. The oasis farmland produces cotton, wheat, corn, pomegranates, pears, apricots and walnuts.

The Book of Han of the 1st century BCE first mentions the territory as Shaju, probably related to the name of the Iranian Saka tribes. In the 1st century CE the kingdom of Suoju was the most powerful in the Western Regions. Its king Xian, given the seal of Protector General in 41 CE and then denied it, conquered Kucha and other kingdoms, until Guangde of Khotan captured him in 61 CE and killed him. The Han general Ban Chao defeated Suoju in 86 CE, and in 130 CE Yarkand sent tribute to the Chinese emperor along with Ferghana and Kashgar.

Little is recorded for many centuries after that. Yarkant became the main base of Chagatai Khan, who inherited Kashgaria after Genghis Khan died in 1227. Marco Polo described it in 1273 as a province where people followed the law of Mahomet, with some Nestorian Christians, and rich in cotton. In 1509 the Dughlats rebelled against Moghulistan, and five years later Sultan Said Khan conquered them and set up the Yarkent Khanate, with Yarkand as its capital. The Jesuit Benedict Göez reached the city in 1603 and called it a mart of much note, where the Kabul caravan ended and a new one formed for Cathay.

The Qing dynasty gained control of the region in the middle of the 18th century. By the 19th century trade with Ladakh and foreign merchants made it the largest and most populous state of Kashgar. In the 1860s Yakub Beg made Yarkant the capital of his Turkic state of Yettishar and received embassies from England in 1870 and 1873. The Qing defeated him in 1877, and he committed suicide. Yarkant is now predominantly Uyghur, with a small Tajik minority.
yaroslav-ii-of-vladimir: Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, baptised Theodore, was born on 8 February 1191, the fourth son of Vsevolod the Big Nest and Maria Shvarnovna. In 1200 his father sent him to rule Pereiaslav near the Kypchak steppes. Six years later the boyars of Halych summoned him to their city, but he could not claim the throne. He was then sent to take Ryazan, and the stubborn opposition of its inhabitants led to the city being burnt. In 1209 Vsevolod sent him against Mstislav the Bold in Novgorod, and after several battles the two made peace and Yaroslav married Mstislav's daughter.

On his deathbed Vsevolod left him Pereslavl-Zalessky. In the quarrel between his elder brothers Konstantin and Yuri he supported Yuri. In 1215 he accepted an offer from the Novgorodians to be their prince, but he captured Torzhok and blocked its grain from Novgorod. He was defeated by his father-in-law on the Lipitsa River, and a helmet he lost there was found by archaeologists in 1808. He returned to Novgorod in 1234, defeated Lithuanians and the Teutonic Knights some years later, and in 1236 moved to Kiev on the advice of Daniel of Galicia, leaving his son Alexander as his representative in the north.

In 1238, when the Mongols first invaded Kievan Rus' and Yuri was killed in battle, Yaroslav left Kiev for Vladimir, where he was crowned grand prince. He tried to restore the cities of Vladimir-Suzdal after the ravages of the Mongol invasion. In 1243 Batu Khan summoned him to Sarai, and after a long conference he returned with honours. Two years later Güyük Khan summoned him to Karakorum.

According to Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Yaroslav ate at the tent of Töregene Khatun, fell ill at once, and died within a week, on 30 September 1246. Carpine reports that everyone believed Töregene had poisoned him in order to conquer his lands, though later historians have disputed the accusation. By his third wife, Fedosia Igorevna of Ryazan, whom he married in 1218, he had at least twelve children, among them Alexander Nevsky, Andrei II of Vladimir, Mikhail Khorobrit, Yaroslav of Tver and Vasily of Kostroma.
yaroslav-the-wise: Little is known of Yaroslav's early years. He was a son of Vladimir the Great, presumably by Rogneda of Polotsk, although his age as stated in the Primary Chronicle, and as shown by the examination of his skeleton in the 1930s, would place him among Vladimir's youngest children. Some scholars have suggested that his mother was in fact Anna Porphyrogenita. In the Norse sagas he appears as Jarisleif the Lame, and his lameness was confirmed by the scientists who examined his remains.

Vladimir sent him to rule the lands around Rostov, and in 1010 he was transferred to Novgorod. There he founded the town of Yaroslavl on the Volga. In 1014 he refused to pay tribute to Kiev. After Vladimir's death in July 1015 he fought a bloody war against his half-brother Sviatopolk I, during which his brothers Boris, Gleb and Svyatoslav were killed. The Primary Chronicle blames Sviatopolk.

Yaroslav defeated Sviatopolk in 1016, lost Kiev to him and his Polish allies in 1018, and firmly established his rule there in 1019. In 1024 his brother Mstislav of Chernigov defeated him, and the two divided the realm along the Dnieper. After Mstislav's death in 1036 Yaroslav ruled the whole of it. He relied on a Scandinavian alliance, married Ingegerd Olofsdotter, daughter of the Swedish king Olof Skötkonung, in 1019, and captured Tartu in 1030, renaming it Yuryev.

To defend against the Pechenegs he built a line of forts, and after his decisive victory over them near Kiev in 1036 he sponsored the building of Saint Sophia Cathedral in 1037. In 1051 he had the monk Hilarion of Kiev made metropolitan, challenging the practice of appointing Greeks. A Rus' fleet sent against Constantinople in 1043 defeated the Byzantine fleet but was nearly destroyed by a storm. The Russkaya Pravda was probably issued during his Novgorod years.

Yaroslav's daughters married into foreign courts: Elisiv to Harald Hardrada, Anastasia to the future Andrew I of Hungary, and Anne to Henry I of France, who acted as regent for her son. Three of his sons, Iziaslav I, Sviatoslav II and Vsevolod I, reigned in Kiev in turn. He urged his sons to live in peace. His sarcophagus in Saint Sophia was opened in 1936 and again in 2009, when it was found to hold only a female skeleton, and his remains are regarded as lost.
yaroslavl: Yaroslavl stands about 250 kilometres north-east of Moscow, at the confluence of the Volga and the Kotorosl. The oldest settlement in the area lies on the left bank of the Volga opposite the Strelka, the small cape where the rivers meet, and dates from the 5th to 3rd millennium BCE. The city belongs to the Golden Ring, a group of historic towns north-east of Moscow that have played an important role in Russian history. Its urban area covers about 205 square kilometres and extends across both rivers.

Yaroslavl is counted the oldest of the surviving towns on the Volga. It was founded by Yaroslav the Wise, a prince of Kievan Rus', while he ruled the Principality of Rostov between 988 and 1010. He landed at the Strelka, a spot protected by the high banks of three rivers, and began the first Kremlin. The first recorded event there was the Rostov Uprising of 1071, which followed a famine. The city is reported to have been the capital of an independent principality from 1218, and it was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1463, formally in 1471.

Fires repeatedly damaged the city in the 16th century, and the old tradition of building in wood gave way to stone. The Spaso-Preobrazhensky monastery, destroyed in 1501, was rebuilt, and its cathedral of 1506 to 1516 is the oldest unchanged building in the city. Ivan the Terrible made several pilgrimages to Yaroslavl, and its two large monasteries gained from rich gifts from his court. In the 17th century the city was Russia's second largest, and in 1612, during the Polish occupation of Moscow, it was for a time the country's de facto capital. Trade on the Volga, and north to Arkhangelsk and east to Siberia, made it wealthy, and leather-working, textiles, fragrances and silverwork flourished.

From 6 to 21 July 1918 the Yaroslavl Rebellion, an armed attempt by conservative activists to remove the new Bolshevik authorities, was crushed by the Red Army after bombardment from artillery and aircraft. Official figures put the deaths among residents at about 600, and some 2,000 buildings were destroyed or badly damaged. Yaroslavl is the administrative centre of Yaroslavl Oblast and a centre of industry, with a population of 577,279 at the 2021 census. Its historic centre is a World Heritage Site.
yashwant-rao-holkar: Yashwant Rao was the third son of Tukoji Rao Holkar. He was educated in accountancy and could read Persian, Marathi and Urdu. On 29 January 1797 Tukoji named his eldest son, Kashi Rao, as his successor. The second son, Malhar Rao, rebelled and Yashwant Rao joined him; on 14 September the army of Daulat Rao Scindia surprised their camp, Malhar Rao was killed and Yashwant Rao fled wounded. He gathered a following that included Pindharis and Afghans under Mir Khan. Claiming to act for his infant nephew Khande Rao, he declared himself head of the Holkars in January 1799, and by April had defeated Kashi Rao's commander, the Chevalier Dudrenec.

In 1799 the widows of Mahadaji Scindia asked his help to recover Ujjain and promised him four lakh rupees; he accepted five lakh from Ambaji Ingle to betray them, and looted the city. His victory over Scindia and the Peshwa on 25 October 1802, the day of Diwali, was won at Hadapsar near Pune. The Peshwa fled to Sinhagad, and Holkar took over the administration at Pune and appointed Amrutrao as Peshwa. The British, fearing for their own territories and those of their ally the Nizam of Hyderabad, decided to restore the Peshwa under their protection.

On 8 October 1804 he marched on Delhi to gain control of the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and besieged it for more than a week, but could not overcome the defence under Colonel Ochterlony. The emperor nevertheless gave him the title Maharajadhiraja Raj Rajeshwar Alija Bahadur. He appealed to other Indian rulers to join him against the British, but Daulat Rao Scindia would not fight and others gave no direct help. He fled to the Sikh Empire, where Ranjit Singh refused a British request to arrest him.

By the treaty signed at Rajghat on 24 December 1805 the British returned his territory, accepted his dominion over Jaipur, Udaipur, Kota and Bundi and undertook not to interfere in Holkar affairs; he gave up his claims to Bundelkhand and the lands north of the Chambal. He thus avoided the subsidiary alliance imposed on other Maratha chiefs. Lord Lake resigned in protest at the abandonment of the Company's Indian allies. In a letter of 15 February 1806 Holkar wrote that he had concluded the war when he found himself abandoned on all sides. He died on 28 October 1811.
yasser-arafat: Arafat was born in Cairo on 4 or 24 August 1929, the second-youngest of seven children of Palestinian parents. His father, Abdel Raouf al-Qudwa al-Husseini, was from Gaza City and worked as a textile merchant in Cairo. His mother, Zahwa Abul Saud, whose family home was Jerusalem, died in 1933. He enrolled at the University of King Fuad I in 1944 and graduated in 1950, and by 1946 was an Arab nationalist procuring weapons to be smuggled into Mandatory Palestine. When the 1948 Arab-Israeli War began he left the university and fought in the Gaza area alongside the Muslim Brotherhood, without joining it. He later served as president of the General Union of Palestinian Students from 1952 to 1956.

After the Suez Crisis of 1956 the guerrilla forces in Gaza were expelled, Arafat among them. In 1957 he obtained a visa for Kuwait, where he met Salah Khalaf and Khalil al-Wazir, who became his top aides. In the late 1950s he co-founded Fatah, a paramilitary organisation seeking Israel's replacement with a Palestinian state, which he led from 1959. He joined the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1967 and in 1969 was elected chair of the Palestinian National Council. Fatah's presence in Jordan brought clashes with King Hussein's government, and in the early 1970s it moved to Lebanon, where it took part in the Lebanese Civil War and became a target of Israeli invasions in 1978 and 1982.

From 1983 to 1993 he was based in Tunisia, and in 1985 survived an Israeli bombing of his Tunis headquarters in which 73 people died. He shifted from open conflict to negotiation, acknowledging Israel's right to exist in 1988, and took part in the Madrid Conference of 1991, the talks that led to the Oslo Accords of 1993 and the Camp David Summit of 2000. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 with Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

After being confined in his Ramallah compound by the Israeli army for over two years, Arafat fell into a coma in late 2004 and died on 11 November 2004; the cause of his death remains the subject of speculation. Palestinians generally view him as a martyr who symbolised their national aspirations, while many Israelis regarded him as a terrorist. Palestinian rivals often denounced him as corrupt or too submissive in his concessions to Israel.
yavne: Yavne lies in the southern coastal plain, about six kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea and on the eastern border of the Yavne sand dunes. The ancient town stood on a natural kurkar hill, now the archaeological site of Tel Yavne, which excavations show to have been inhabited continuously from the Bronze or Iron Age until the British Mandate. The name appears in many English translations of the Bible as Jabneh, in Greek and Latin sources as Jamnia, and in the Ottoman and British periods as Yibna. The ancient town had a long history of wine production.

In Roman times King Herod bequeathed Iamnia to his sister Salome, and it then passed to Emperor Augustus, who ran it as a private imperial estate. In 68 CE, after Vespasian had put down the revolt in Galilee, his army took the town and garrisoned it. According to rabbinic tradition, Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai obtained Vespasian's permission to settle there and teach his disciples, and after the fall of Jerusalem his school functioned as a Sanhedrin. A supposed Council of Jamnia that fixed the Jewish biblical canon was long theorised, but current scholarship largely rejects it.

The Crusaders called the town Ibelin and built a castle there in 1141. Its namesake family, the House of Ibelin, was important in the Kingdom of Jerusalem and later in the Kingdom of Cyprus. Saladin sacked it before his army was routed at the Battle of Montgisard in 1177, and in August 1187 it was retaken and burnt. The parish church became a mosque, and a minaret was added in the Mamluk period in 1337. During the 1948 war most of the villagers of Yibna fled, and the Israeli troops that arrived on 5 June found the village almost deserted.

Modern Yavne was founded in October 1948 as a transit camp for Jews from Arab countries, Iran and Europe, and the first neighbourhood followed in early 1949. It received city status in 1986 and lies in the Central District of Israel. The minaret of the old mosque still stands, and excavations at Tel Yavne since 2005 have uncovered the gate room of the Crusader castle.
yazd: Yazd is the capital of Yazd province in central Iran, and its name means pure or holy, the city's name meaning City of the Holy One. Former names include Kath and Isatis. It has a hot desert climate and is the driest major city in Iran, with under 60 millimetres of rain a year and summer days frequently above 40 °C. Generations of adaptation to this setting gave it its wind towers, large underground rooms, cisterns called ab anbars, ice stores called yakhchals and one of the largest networks of qanats, underground water channels, in the world. It is also one of the largest cities built almost entirely of adobe.

Archaeological evidence north of the city suggests settlement from the Achaemenid period, and some scholars link the name to the Issatis that Pliny the Elder places in the Parthian Empire. Yazd gained prominence under the Sasanian Empire. Yazdegerd I (r. 399–420) established a mint there, and a chronicle of 1441 says it was re-founded by Yazdegerd II. After the Muslim conquest many Zoroastrians moved to Yazd, and by paying a levy it was allowed to stay Zoroastrian, with Islam becoming dominant only gradually.

Its isolated desert position spared it much warfare, and it was a haven for people fleeing the Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire.
