Marco Polo visited in 1272 and praised its trade and its silk cloth, called Yasdi. In the 14th century it was briefly the capital of the Muzaffarid dynasty and was unsuccessfully besieged in 1350–1351 by the Injuids under Abu Ishaq Inju. Under the Qajar Empire it was ruled by the Bakhtiari Khans.

The population was 529,673 at the 2016 census. Most people are Persians who speak a Yazdi accent, and most are Shia Muslims, with a Zoroastrian minority of around 1,000 in 600,000. Zoroastrian heritage includes a Tower of Silence on the outskirts and a temple fire said to have burned continuously since 470 CE. The oldest dated building is the 11th-century Davāzdah Imām mausoleum, and the Jame Mosque has the country's highest minarets. The silk and carpet trade of the past continues in textiles, ceramics and confectionery. The historic city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.
yazdegerd-ii: Yazdegerd II succeeded his father, Bahram V, in 438. The Romans had agreed in a treaty of 387 to share the defence of the Caucasus against nomadic attacks, and paid roughly 500 pounds of gold at irregular intervals, which they saw as a subsidy and the Iranians as tribute. When Theodosius II declined to continue, Yazdegerd declared war, with little success for either side. Vandal attacks on the Roman south led Theodosius to send Anatolius to the Sasanian camp, and in 440 both empires promised not to build new fortifications in Mesopotamia.

In the east the Kidarites and other groups known as Iranian Huns had long pressed the empire, and had forced Iran to pay tribute, which Yazdegerd refused. In 450 he led an expedition deep into Kidarite territory, taking forts, cities, captives and wealth. In 453 he moved his court to Nishapur and left his minister Mihr Narseh in charge of the empire. His forces first suffered a severe defeat, and the war continued for many years. He fortified Damghan as a border post.

Armenian and Syriac sources portray Yazdegerd as a religious fanatic, while Arabic and Persian sources show a pious king who clashed with the aristocracy. Persecution of Christians began in 446 with the nobles of Karkh and spread to Iberia and Armenia, and the Armenian rebellion led by Vardan Mamikonian was defeated and Vardan killed at Avarayr on 2 June 451, with heavy Sasanian losses. Afterwards religious freedom was allowed. Jews were persecuted too, reportedly with a ban on open observance of the Sabbath. Modern historians such as Eberhard Sauer and Scott McDonough doubt that he was a zealot, and McDonough suggests Zoroastrianism may have been a test of personal loyalty.

He was the first Sasanian ruler to take the title kay, linking the dynasty to the mythical Kayanians of the Avesta, and his coins read mazdesn bay kay. In the 440s he had a mudbrick defensive system built at Derbent to hold off incursions from the north, and a later chronicle credits him with refounding the city of Yazd.

He died in 457, reportedly without naming a successor, and civil war followed between his sons. Hormizd III took the throne at Ray, while Peroz fled north-east and raised an army, and their mother, Denag, ruled temporarily as regent from Ctesiphon. Peroz emerged victorious. Persian sources generally praise Yazdegerd as an astute and well-read ruler, known to Ibn al-Balkhi and Hamza al-Isfahani as Yazdegerd the Gentle, a favourable account that is tied to a policy of persecuting non-Zoroastrians, which appeased the aristocracy and the Zoroastrian priesthood.
yazdegerd-iii: Yazdegerd was the son of the prince Shahriyar and the grandson of Khosrow II, the last prominent shah of Iran. Khosrow was overthrown and executed in 628 by his own son Kavad II, who ordered the execution of all his brothers and half-brothers, including Shahriyar. A civil war of four years followed, and a plague killed half the population of the western provinces. After a succession of short-lived rulers, the magnates Rostam Farrokhzad and Piruz Khosrow allied and installed Yazdegerd, who had been hiding at Istakhr. He was crowned in the Temple of Anahita there, where Ardashir I had crowned himself four centuries earlier. Most scholars agree he was eight years old.

The boy lacked authority, and army commanders, courtiers and aristocrats fought each other in often deadly feuds. Regional governors declared independence, and the Pahlav faction in the north at first refused to mint his coins. The empire was also raided by the Göktürks in the east and the Khazars in the west. In 633 Muslim Arabs defeated a Sasanian force near Hira. In 636 the Sasanian army under Rostam was crushed at al-Qadisiyyah, and Rostam was killed. The Arabs reached Ctesiphon in 637 and occupied it, while Yazdegerd fled with the treasury to Hulwan.

He raised a new army in Media, which was defeated at the Battle of Nahavand in 642, and then fled to Isfahan and Istakhr. In 650 Abdullah ibn Aamir of Basra invaded Pars, and 40,000 defenders were reported killed. Yazdegerd moved on to Kirman and Sakastan, where his demands for taxes and his manner alienated the local governors. He sent envoys to Tang China from 638 to 648 seeking help, but the Chinese sent assistance only after his death.

Yazdegerd was killed in 651 by a miller near Merv, either for his jewellery or, according to The Cambridge History of Iran, at the instigation of the local margrave Mahoe. By tradition he was buried at Merv by Christian monks. His death ended more than four centuries of Sasanian rule and the last pre-Islamic Iranian empire, and made the conquest of the rest of Iran easier. He is remembered as a martyred prince, and many later rulers and officers of Islamic Iran claimed descent from him. The Zoroastrian religious calendar still uses the year of his reign as its base year.
yazid-i: Yazid was born in Syria; the year of his birth is uncertain and falls between 642 and 649. His father was Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, then governor of Syria and later caliph. His mother, Maysun, was the daughter of a chieftain of the Banu Kalb and, like most of her tribe, a Christian. Yazid grew up among his Kalbite kin in the Syrian Desert and, for the rest of the year, among the Greek and native Syrian courtiers of his father. In Mu'awiya's reign he led several campaigns against the Byzantine Empire, including an attack on Constantinople.

In 676 his father nominated him heir, the first hereditary succession in the history of the caliphate, and several grandees of the Hejaz, among them Husayn ibn Ali and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, opposed it.

Mu'awiya died in April 680. Husayn and Ibn al-Zubayr refused to recognise Yazid and took refuge in Mecca. Husayn left for Kufa to lead a revolt and was killed with his small band of followers in the Battle of Karbala. His death caused widespread resentment in the Hejaz. Ibn al-Zubayr declared Yazid deposed, and the people of Medina renounced their allegiance and expelled the Umayyads living in the city. Yazid sent an army of 12,000 men under Muslim ibn Uqba, which defeated the Medinans at the Battle of al-Harra in August 683. Accounts differ on whether the city was plundered. His army then besieged Mecca for several weeks from September 683, during which the Ka'ba caught fire.

Yazid continued his father's decentralised style of government, relying on provincial governors and tribal nobles. He kept officials such as Ibn Ziyad and the Christian Sarjun ibn Mansur, abandoned the raids against the Byzantines and made no new conquests. He dug a canal, known as Nahr Yazid, to improve irrigation in the Ghouta near Damascus.

Yazid died on 11 November 683 at Huwwarin in the Syrian desert, his favourite residence, and the siege of Mecca ended. The caliphate then fell into a civil war of nearly a decade. Many Muslims regard him as an illegitimate ruler and a tyrant, and for the Shia he is an epitome of evil, reviled in the Ashura processions. Modern historians take a milder view and consider him a capable ruler, though less successful than his father. The killing of Husayn contributed to the formation of Shia identity.
yazidis: The Yazidis are a Kurdish-speaking endogamous religious group indigenous to Kurdistan, with small numbers in Armenia and Georgia. Scholars and Yazidis themselves disagree on whether they are a distinct ethnoreligious group or a religious sub-group of the Kurds. Yazidism took shape from a pre-Islamic Kurdish religious substratum, given its lasting doctrinal and institutional form by the reforms and teachings of Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir and his successors in the 12th and 13th centuries. Scholars have proposed several sources for the older substratum, from Indo-Iranian traditions shared with Zoroastrianism to ancient Mesopotamian religion and Hellenistic currents. Earlier descriptions of Yazidism as an offshoot of Islam have been widely given up.

Yazidis call themselves Êzidî. Some Western scholars derive the name from the Umayyad caliph Yazid I, which Yazidis reject. Other derivations link it to Old Iranian yazata or Middle Persian yazad, divine being, or to the phrase meaning God created me.

Yazidis first came into contact with the Ottomans in the early 16th century and lived as semi-independent groups within the empire. In 1516, after Selim the Grim took Aleppo from the Mamluks, the Yazidi Sheikh Izz ed-Din had himself named Emir of the Kurds there by having the Ottoman governors execute his rival Qasim Beg for treason; when he died without heirs the title returned to Qasim Beg's family.

Under Abdul Hamid II, loyalty was increasingly measured by Muslim identity, and conscription was used to push conversion. Omer Wehbi Pasha, sent to Mosul, used violence against Yazidis who would not cooperate. About 500 Yazidis died in the Shingal campaign of November–December 1892, Lalish was turned into a madrasah and sacred objects were confiscated. Refugees on Shingal mountain spread accounts of the atrocities, and a religious revival followed, with preaching of an imminent reign of justice. In 2014 the Islamic State captured Sinjar, and over 5,000 Yazidis were killed, thousands of women and girls enslaved and more than 500,000 people displaced.

Yazidi cultural practices and almost all of their orally transmitted religious traditions are in Kurmanji, though the Yazidis of Bashiqa and Bahzani speak Arabic. Yazidis marry only other Yazidis, and those who marry outside the community are expelled. Most Yazidis in the Middle East live in Iraq, chiefly in Nineveh and Duhok, in the Shekhan and Sinjar districts, where the shrine of Sheikh Adi stands at Lalish. Large communities also exist in Armenia, where 35,272 were counted in 2011, and in Germany, where over 230,000 live. Some followers of other monotheistic faiths equate the Peacock Angel with Satan, which has led to centuries of persecution of Yazidis as devil worshippers.
yellow-river: The Yellow River, or Huang He, is the second-longest river in China and the sixth-longest in the world, an estimated 5,464 kilometres long with a drainage basin of 795,000 square kilometres. It rises in the Bayan Har Mountains and flows generally eastwards, makes the 1,500-kilometre Ordos Loop through Inner Mongolia, turns south to form the border between Shanxi and Shaanxi, turns east again at its confluence with the Wei River and crosses the North China Plain to the Bohai Sea. It is named for the yellow colour of its water, from the sediment it carries from the Loess Plateau. Chronicles indicate that the river, once simply called the river, became muddy sometime between 367 BCE and 165 CE.

The basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese civilisation. According to traditional historiography the Xia dynasty originated on its banks around 2100 BCE, and Sima Qian's Shiji records that the Xia were founded after the tribes around the river united to fight its floods. One estimate counts 1,593 floods in the 2,540 years between 595 BCE and 1946, and the river has been nicknamed both China's Pride and China's Sorrow.

In 602 BCE it shifted several hundred kilometres east at Suxu Mouth, the first major course change recorded in history. In 1128 Song troops under the Kaifeng governor Du Chong breached the southern dikes to stop the advancing Jin army, and the river shifted south of the Shandong Peninsula into the Yellow Sea, where it flowed until 1855, merging with the Huai River. Between 1851 and 1855 it returned north, amid floods that provoked the Nien and Taiping Rebellions, and it more or less adopted its present course in the flood of 1897.

Floods of the river have killed over one million people in all. Among the deadliest were the flood of 1344 under the Yuan dynasty, the flood of 1887, which killed between 900,000 and 2 million people, and the flood of 1931, which killed an estimated 1 to 4 million and is the worst recorded flood by deaths. Flooding in 1898 left whole communities in Shandong destitute and, with the drought that followed, contributed to the rise of the Boxer movement. About 120 million people live in the basin, which holds 13 per cent of China's cultivated land.
yellow-sea: The Yellow Sea is a marginal sea of the Western Pacific. Excluding the Bohai, it extends about 960 km from north to south and about 700 km from east to west, with an area of approximately 380,000 km2 and an average depth of only 44 m; its maximum depth is 152 m. It is a section of continental shelf that was flooded after the last glacial period, some 10,000 years ago, when sea levels rose by 120 m.

Its innermost bay, the Bohai Sea, receives the Yellow River, the Hai River and the Liao River. The Korea Bay, its north-eastern extension, receives the Yalu, the Chongchon and the Taedong. Sand and silt from these rivers, together with sand storms, give the water its golden-yellow colour. The sea is one of four named after colour terms, the others being the Black, Red and White Seas. Koreans call it the West Sea, one of three seas around the peninsula.

Chinese, Korean and Japanese ships have fished its waters for centuries. The bottom layers are rich in fish, and about 200 species have been exploited commercially, among them sea bream, croakers, prawns, cutlassfish, squid, eel and Pacific herring. Navigation is another traditional activity, and the coasts are densely populated, at about 250 inhabitants per square kilometre.

The sea has a cold, dry winter, with strong northerly monsoons from late November to March, and a wet, warm summer with frequent typhoons between June and October. In the north, drift ice and continuous ice fields form and hinder navigation between November and March. Tides are semidiurnal and run higher on the Korean side, from 4 to 8 metres, than on the Chinese coast, where the range is about 0.9 to 3 metres. The fastest tidal currents, up to 20 km/h, occur in the Myeongnyang Strait between Jindo Island and the Korean Peninsula.

Near Jindo, tidal variation opens a land passage 2.9 km long between Jindo and Modo islands for about an hour, twice a year, in early May and mid-June. A local festival has long marked it, though it was little known abroad until 1975.

The main Chinese ports on the sea are Dalian, Tianjin, Yantai, Qingdao, Tangshan and Qinhuangdao. The major South Korean ports are Incheon, Gunsan and Mokpo, and North Korea's is Nampho, the outport of Pyongyang. The Bohai Train Ferry gives a shortcut between the Liaodong Peninsula and Shandong.

The southern part, including the whole west coast of Korea, holds a belt of intertidal mudflats 10 km wide with an area of 2,850 km2. They are the most important site for migratory birds on northward migration in the East Asian–Australasian Flyway. Spotted seals are the only resident seal species, and a sanctuary for them lies at Baengnyeongdo.
yellow-turban-rebellion: By 184 the central government of the Han dynasty was weakened by court eunuchs who abused their power over the emperor to enrich themselves. Corruption was seen as the cause of plagues, natural disasters and poor harvests, a sign that the emperor had lost the Mandate of Heaven. Flooding along the Yellow River drove farmers south, and the surplus of labour encouraged exploitation.

The rebels followed the Way of Supreme Peace, led by Zhang Jue and his younger brothers Zhang Bao and Zhang Liang, who had founded a Taoist sect in what is now Shandong and were praised as healers who treated poor patients free of charge. They held that an apocalyptic change would come in the jiazi year, the start of a new sexagenary cycle. Their slogan said that the Azure Sky was dead and the Yellow Sky would rise, which gave them the colour of their headwear.

A few days before the planned rising, one of the sect's founders, Tang Zhou, betrayed the plot, and the organiser Ma Yuanyi was arrested and executed in Luoyang. In March 184 Zhang Jue began the rebellion with roughly 360,000 followers, calling himself the Lord General of Heaven. The rebels attacked government offices, pillaged villages and seized commanderies, and within ten days the rising had spread across China.

Han forces under Huangfu Song, Zhu Jun and Lu Zhi fought the main rebel armies. By the start of 185 the rebellion had mostly been suppressed, and in mid-February the emperor changed his era name to Zhongping, meaning pacification achieved. Remnants rose again for two decades. The White Wave Bandits appeared in 188, and in 192 hundreds of thousands of Yellow Turban remnants who entered Yan Province surrendered to Cao Cao, who made the best of them into the elite Qingzhou Army.

The rebellion destroyed major government buildings, killed high officials and fragmented the dynasty's territory. Rebel deaths numbered in the hundreds of thousands, and many civilians were left homeless or destitute. The court's weakness and the rising political influence of regional military governors who helped suppress it led to warlord dominance and the Three Kingdoms period. After Emperor Ling died in 189, Dong Zhuo took control of the young heir and the capital, and the Han dynasty collapsed completely by 220. The revolt also marks an important point in the history of Taoism, and it is the inciting event of the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
yemelyan-pugachev: Pugachev was the youngest son of a small Don Cossack landowner and was born in the stanitsa of Zimoveyskaya, in present-day Volgograd Oblast. He enlisted at 17, married a Cossack girl, Sofya Nedyuzheva, within the year, and joined the Russian army in Prussia during the Seven Years' War. He returned home in 1762 and reached the Cossack rank of khorunzhiy. At the siege of Bender in 1770, during the Russo-Turkish War, he first showed a flair for impersonation by telling comrades that his sword was a gift from his godfather, Peter I.

In 1770 he left the army and became a fugitive. He was arrested and escaped several times, spent time among the Cossacks of the Terek, and returned to Russia in the autumn of 1772 with the help of Old Believers. He settled near present-day Volsk and probably heard there of the rebellion of the Yaik Cossacks.

The idea of posing as the dead Emperor Peter III came to Pugachev early. Peter III had been overthrown and murdered in 1762 by supporters of his wife, the future Catherine II. Pugachev promised to restore privileges to the Cossacks and the Old Belief, and in 1773 he began an open revolt, proclaiming an end to serfdom. His army overran much of the region between the Volga and the Urals, and he gained the support of industrial peasants in the Urals. He set up a College of War with four judges to organise his army, and it paid wages and bounties to the Cossacks. His chief success was the capture of Kazan in 1774, where the city was burned to the ground.

General Pyotr Panin was slow to act against him, because of transport difficulties and indiscipline among his poorly paid soldiers. In August 1774 General Michelsohn crushed the rebels near Tsaritsyn, and about ten thousand were killed or taken prisoner. Panin carried out savage reprisals after the capture of Penza. On 14 September 1774 Pugachev's own Cossacks handed him over at Yaitsk.

Alexander Suvorov had him placed in an iron cage and sent to Simbirsk and then to Moscow. He was executed publicly in Bolotnaya Square on 21 January 1775, beheaded and then quartered. Catherine II had been trying to reform the provincial administration, but the horrors of the revolt made her drop other reforms, in particular attempts to emancipate the serfs. Alexander Pushkin wrote a history of the rebellion and used it in his novel The Captain's Daughter (1836).
yemen: Yemen lies in southern Arabia and covers 455,503 square kilometres, with a coastline of about 2,000 kilometres. It borders Saudi Arabia to the north and Oman to the northeast, and its territory includes the Socotra Archipelago and several Red Sea islands, among them the Hanish Islands, Kamaran and Perim. Socotra lies east of the Horn of Africa and is geographically and bio-geographically associated with Africa.

The country divides into four main regions: the coastal plains in the west, the western highlands, the eastern highlands and the Rub' al Khali in the east. The Tihamah, a very arid and flat plain along the Red Sea coast, ends abruptly at the escarpment of the western highlands. These highlands are heavily terraced and receive the highest rainfall in Arabia, from about 760 millimetres a year at Taiz to over 1,000 millimetres at Ibb.

Large settlements existed in the mountains of northern Yemen from about 5000 BCE. The four major kingdoms of South Arabia were Saba, Hadhramaut, Qataban and Ma'in. Saba, thought to be the biblical Sheba, was the most prominent, and its rulers took a title generally thought to mean unifier. It built the Great Dam of Marib around 940 BCE. A Roman army of 10,000 men under Aelius Gallus was defeated before it reached Marib.

By the third century BCE Qataban, Hadhramaut and Ma'in had become independent of Saba, which regained its hegemony after Qataban collapsed in 50 BCE. The Himyarites annexed Sanaa around 100 CE, and by 275 Shammar Yahri'sh had conquered Hadhramaut, Najran and Tihamah, unifying Yemen under Himyarite rule. By 515 Himyar was divided along religious lines, and civil turmoil brought an intervention from Aksum.

Islam spread rapidly in the seventh century, and for centuries Yemen was a primary producer of coffee, exported through the port of Mokha. In the nineteenth century the country was divided between the Ottoman and British empires. The Kingdom of Yemen was established after the First World War and became the Yemen Arab Republic in 1962. South Yemen became independent in 1967, and the two states united in 1990.

Sanaa is the constitutional capital and largest city. Modern Standard Arabic is the official language and Islam the state religion. The country has an estimated population of about 34.7 million. The old city of Sanaa, with its tower-houses of mud-brick and stone, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Yemen is a member of the Arab League, the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
yemeni-civil-war-2014-present: Islam in Yemen takes mainly Sunni and Shia forms, and among the Shia the Ismaili and Zaydi sects historically competed for influence. After the Ayyubid expansion most of the Hamdan tribe converted to Zaydism, and during the Rasulid period, from 1229 to 1454, Shafi'i Sunni Islam gained popularity. From the 1960s Zaydis faced discrimination under governments that favoured Sunni Islam. The Houthis, or Ansar Allah, are a Zaydi group from the Sa'dah Governorate on Yemen's northern border with Saudi Arabia, who led a low-level insurgency against the government from 2004 after their leader, Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, was killed in a military crackdown.

After weeks of street protests against the administration of President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, which had cut fuel subsidies, the Houthis fought army forces under General Ali Mohsen al-Ahmar and in a battle of a few days took Sanaa in September 2014. Hadi negotiated an agreement under which the government resigned and the Houthis gained unprecedented influence over state institutions.

On 21 March 2015 the Houthi-led Supreme Revolutionary Committee declared a general mobilization. With forces loyal to the former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, the Houthis fought in Lahij Governorate and by 25 March had reached the outskirts of Aden, where Hadi's government sat. Hadi fled the country the same day. A coalition led by Saudi Arabia began air strikes and other operations to restore the government. Aden was recaptured, but the conflict settled into a protracted stalemate.

Saleh was assassinated in 2017 after his alliance with the Houthis broke down. The Southern Transitional Council, formed in 2017 and backed by the United Arab Emirates, captured Aden in 2018, and clashes followed between it and forces loyal to Hadi, who were backed by Saudi Arabia. The Stockholm Agreement of December 2018 sought a ceasefire around Hodeida. A United Nations truce began in April 2022.

The war brought a severe humanitarian crisis. The United Nations reports more than 150,000 people killed, and estimates of more than 227,000 further deaths from famine and the lack of health care. Yemen meets 90% of its food needs through imports, and a blockade disrupted deliveries, while cholera cases rose from 2015. The UN Security Council imposed an arms embargo on the Houthis in 2015.
yenisei-river: The Yenisei is the fifth-longest river system in the world and the largest to drain into the Arctic Ocean. The river proper is 3,487 km long, measured from the meeting of the Great Yenisei and Little Yenisei at Kyzyl to its mouth in the Kara Sea. Its basin covers 2,580,000 km2 and includes Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake. It divides the Western Siberian Plain from the Central Siberian Plateau and flows through Tuva, Khakassia and Krasnoyarsk Krai. The basin holds 55 native fish species, two of them endemic.

Nomadic peoples such as the Ket and the Yugh have lived along the banks since ancient times, and the region is the home of the Yeniseian language family. The Ket, about 1,000 in number, are the only survivors of those who once lived throughout central southern Siberia, and were politically absorbed into Russia between the 17th and 19th centuries. Some of the earliest evidence of Turkic origins was found in the valley, in stelae and memorial tablets of the seventh to ninth centuries.

The river's first written mention, as Kem, dates to the 7th century in Tang dynasty China, at the time of contact with the Yenisei Kyrgyz, and the word Käm appears in 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions. The origin of the name Yenisei remains unclear. Dutch navigators knew the river by the end of the 16th century. Russians reached the lower river from the north-west by 1600, when the Tobolsk Cossacks built Fort Mangazeya, and the upper river in 1605, travelling from the Ob by way of the Ket.

River steamers first came to the Yenisei in 1864, brought across the Kara Sea from the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The Thames overwintered in 1876 and was wrecked, while the Frazer and Express succeeded in 1878. The Dalman reached Yeniseisk in 1881. Captain Joseph Wiggins sailed the Orestes with rails in 1893 during the building of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

The route proved very difficult, since the long estuaries of the Ob and Yenisei are shallow, ice-bound and prone to high winds, and several ships were lost. After the railway was completed, river traffic fell to local service, as the Arctic route was too indirect. Radioactive discharges from a plutonium plant at the secret city of Krasnoyarsk-26, now Zheleznogorsk, contaminated the river.
yeongjo-of-joseon: Yeongjo, personal name Yi Geum, was the second son of King Sukjong, and his life was marked by political infighting and by resentment over the low birth of his mother, Concubine Suk. When his elder half-brother Gyeongjong became king in 1720, the Noron faction unsuccessfully pressed Gyeongjong to step down in his favour.

A few months later Prince Yeoning was named Crown Prince Brother, which sharpened the power struggle and led to the Shinim literati purge of 1721. When Gyeongjong died on 11 October 1724, the Soron accused Yeoning of involvement, though many historians now think food poisoning more likely. He took the throne on 16 October 1724.

Early in his reign the Noron faction regained its position, and a coalition of radical Namin and excluded Soron began Yi In-jwa's Rebellion, which started on 15 March 1728 with the seizure of Cheongju Castle. The royal army defeated the rebels as they marched towards Hanyang, and Yi In-jwa and his family were executed. Yeongjo pursued the Tangpyeong policy of recruiting equally from the factions, believing factional strife harmful. He halved the military service tax, replacing the lost revenue with taxes on fisheries, salt and vessels and an additional land tax, adopted an accounting system for the state's finances and encouraged coinage.

He distributed books in Hangul, including the Book of Agriculture, and had rain gauges made and sent to local offices. Trade grew in Hanseong, and guilds and monopolies expanded. In 1758 he outlawed Catholicism, the first king to act against it. He valued Park Mun-su, whom he made a secret royal inspector to arrest corrupt local officers.

The Annals of the Joseon dynasty record him reducing the dishes on his table in years of flood or famine. In July 1762 he ordered his son Crown Prince Sado into a wooden rice chest, where Sado died on the eighth day; the memoirs of his widow and the Annals report that Sado suffered from mental illness.

Yeongjo was in poor health for much of his life and took many precautions to protect it. He died on 22 April 1776 and is buried with his second wife, Queen Jeongsun, at Wonneung in Guri. His grandson Yi San, the son of Sado, succeeded him as King Jeongjo.

Yeongjo had registered the boy as the son of the late Crown Prince Hyojang to protect his claim. Confucianization was at its height under Yeongjo and Jeongjo, and the economy recovered from the wars of the late 16th and early 17th centuries, but his policies could not hold back the social change that followed.
yeonsangun-of-joseon: Yeonsangun, personal name Yi Yung, was born on 2 December 1476, the eldest surviving son of King Seongjong and the Deposed Queen Yun. Lady Yun had been Seongjong's concubine and was chosen as his second wife for her beauty. She was jealous of the other concubines, poisoned one of them in 1477, and in 1479 struck the king and left scratch marks. Seongjong's mother ordered her into exile, officials later petitioned for her execution, and she died in 1482, ordered to drink poison. The crown prince grew up believing that he was the son of Queen Jeonghyeon, his father's third wife.

In his early years on the throne Yeonsangun was an able administrator who strengthened the national defence and aided the poor. When he learned the truth about his mother he tried to restore her titles, but officials of the Sarim faction opposed him. In 1498 a passage critical of King Sejo's coup of 1455 was put into the royal records, and the king ordered the execution of many Sarim officials and the mutilation of the remains of Kim Chong-jik: the First Literati Purge.

In 1504 Im Sa-hong showed him a blood-stained garment from his mother's death. Yeonsangun beat to death two of his father's concubines, and had officials who had backed his mother's execution put to death, and even those merely present at court: the Second Literati Purge.

He closed the royal university Sungkyunkwan and the temple Wongaksa and made them pleasure grounds, gathering young girls from the eight provinces, and evicted 20,000 residents of the capital to clear hunting grounds. He abolished the Office of Censors. On 19 July 1504 three notices in Hangul mocking his tyranny were found, and he banned the learning and use of the script and ordered those using it beheaded. The author was never caught, and the ban was short-lived.

In September 1506 a group of officials, among them Pak Wŏnjong, Sŏng Hŭian and Yu Sunjŏng, deposed him and set his younger half-brother Grand Prince Jinseong on the throne. Demoted to Prince Yeonsan, he was exiled to Ganghwa Island, where he died after two months. His four young sons were made to take poison. As a much-despised overthrown king he received no temple name.
yerba-mate: The Guaraní and some Tupi communities first cultivated and consumed yerba mate before European colonization. Its use was at first confined to the natives of two regions of what became Paraguay, Amambay and Alto Paraná. The Guaraní name for the plant is kaʼa, meaning herb, while mate comes from the Quechua mati, a word for a container for a drink and for a gourd. The French botanist Augustin Saint-Hilaire named the plant.

Consumption became widespread under Spanish colonization, particularly in the colony of Paraguay in the late 16th century, among settlers and Guaraní alike. It became Paraguay's main commodity, above tobacco, and the labour of indigenous peoples was used to harvest wild stands. In the mid-17th century the Jesuits domesticated the plant and set up plantations in their reductions in Misiones, Argentina. After their expulsion in the 1770s the plantations decayed and their methods of domestication were lost.

Ilex paraguariensis begins as a shrub and matures into a tree up to 15 metres tall. Its evergreen leaves have serrated margins and contain caffeine and related alkaloids, with caffeine making up between 0.7% and 1.7% of dry weight. The flowers are small and greenish-white, and the fruit is a small red drupe. When the plant is harvested the branches are often dried over a wood fire, which gives a smoky flavour. The War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870) devastated Paraguay's economy, and Brazil and Argentina later became the main producers.

Mate is made by filling a container, traditionally a small hollowed-out gourd, up to three-quarters with dry leaves and adding water at 70 to 80 °C, hot but not boiling. With cold water the infusion is called tereré, and the Guaraní drank it in this form, without ice. Drinking mate is a common social practice, often a communal ritual, in Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina, southern Brazil and southern Chile. Friends and family share one gourd and drink through the same straw, called a bombilla. The brewer refills the gourd and passes it round clockwise, and it is also popular in Syria and Lebanon through Syrian immigrants to Argentina.
yerevan: Yerevan lies on the banks of the Hrazdan River, in the north-east of the Ararat Plain, in the central-western part of Armenia and the heart of the Armenian Highland. Its average height is 990 metres. The upper part of the city is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and the Hrazdan divides it in two through a canyon. Mount Ararat, visible from any part of the city, is its principal symbol.

The origin of the name is unknown. One theory ties it to the Armenian king Yervand (Orontes) IV, but it more likely derives from the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BCE, and the name evolved through Erevani and Erevan into Yerevan as Urartian and Armenian elements blended.

The territory has been inhabited since approximately the second half of the 4th millennium BCE. The southern district of Shengavit was populated from at least 3200 BCE in the period of the Kura–Araxes culture of the early Bronze Age, and excavations there found a series of large round buildings and ritual installations. King Argishti I of Urartu founded the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BCE at the western extreme of the Ararat Plain, as a great administrative and religious centre. By the late ancient Armenian Kingdom new capital cities were founded and Yerevan declined.

The Safavid Empire forcibly deported hundreds of thousands of Armenians to Iran in the Great Surgun of 1603–05, which mostly depopulated the city. An earthquake mostly destroyed it in 1679, and it was rebuilt on a smaller scale. It later became part of the Russian Empire. After the First World War it became the capital of the First Republic of Armenia in 1918, as thousands of survivors of the Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire arrived. It grew rapidly in the 20th century within the Soviet Union.

Yerevan is the capital and largest city of Armenia and one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with 1,086,677 people. It has been the capital since 1918, the fourteenth in Armenia's history. It is the seat of the Araratian Pontifical Diocese, the largest diocese of the Armenian Apostolic Church.

Erebuni Fortress is considered the birthplace of the city, and Saint Gregory Cathedral is the largest Armenian cathedral in the world. Tsitsernakaberd is the official memorial to the victims of the Armenian genocide. The Matenadaran holds one of the largest depositories of ancient books and manuscripts in the world.
yermak-timofeyevich: Little is securely known of Yermak. No contemporary description exists, and the Remezov Chronicle, written more than a hundred years after his death, describes his looks although its narrator never saw him. The main sources are the Stroganov Chronicle, commissioned by the Stroganov family and so exaggerating their part, and the Sinodnik, written forty years after his death by Archbishop Cyprian of Tobolsk, who wished to have him canonized. The only account of his upbringing is the Cherepanov Chronicle, compiled by a Tobolsk coachman in 1760, which says he was born by the Chusovaya River and that his grandfather came from Suzdal.

According to that chronicle his father Timofey moved to the Stroganov lands on the Chusovaya, and Yermak worked on the Stroganovs' river fleet as a porter and sailor carrying salt along the Kama and Volga. He then gathered a gang and moved to the Don region as a river pirate, where he acquired the nickname Yermak. Before Siberia his combat experience consisted of leading a Cossack detachment for the tsar in the Livonian War of 1558-83 and plundering merchant ships.

In 1552 the army of Ivan the Terrible toppled the Khanate of Kazan, and the tsar granted the Stroganov merchant family the province of Perm and permission to expand along the Tobol and Irtysh rivers, which belonged to Kuchum Khan. Yermak led a force of 840 men, 540 of his own followers and 300 supplied by the Stroganovs, made up of Russians, Tatars, Lithuanians and Germans. W. Bruce Lincoln describes matchlock muskets, sabers, pikes and small cannons set against Tatar bows, arrows and spears, while Yuri Semyonov says Yermak had no cannon and only a few firearms. On 26 October 1582 he overthrew Kuchum's power at Qashliq and went on fighting the Tatars in Siberia.

Accounts of his death differ. The most common says Kuchum leaked false news that Bukharan merchants were held up on the river. Yermak set out to free them, camped on an island in the Irtysh without posting a guard, and Kuchum's men attacked at night in a storm and killed nearly all of his party. Legend says Yermak drowned, weighed down by armor the tsar had given him. The survivors left Qashliq, reinforcements arrived, and the Russians founded Tyumen in 1586 and Tobolsk in 1587. A monument to him was begun in 1903 at Novocherkassk, and two icebreakers have been named after him.
yesugei: Yesügei, also called Yesükhei Baghatur, belonged to the Borjigin family, and his name means "like nine": he was held to have the auspicious qualities of nine, a lucky number to the Mongols. He was the son of Bartan Baghatur, the second son of Khabul Khan, whom the Jin dynasty recognised as a khagan. Khabul was in turn the great-grandson of the Mongol chief Khaidu, the first to try to unite the Mongols.

With the help of his elder brother Negün Taishi and his younger brother Daritai Otchigin, Yesügei abducted Hö'elün, a daughter of the Olkhunut forest people, from her newlywed husband Chiledu of the Merkits. She became his chief wife. He had four sons by her, Temüjin (later Genghis Khan), Qasar, Hachiun and Temüge, and a daughter, Temülün.

Yesügei was a major chief of the Khamag Mongol confederation. After its khan Hotula died, the confederation had no elected king, but Yesügei ruled it in practice. He had a blood brother, or anda, in Toghrul Khan, later known as Wang Khan and Ong Khan, and helped Toghrul defeat his uncle Gurkhan.

By his second wife Sochigel he had two more sons, Behter and Belgutei. The Secret History of the Mongols records that Temüjin and Qasar, in their youth, ambushed their half brother Behter after he withheld the spoils of hunts and shot him with arrows, sparing Belgutei at Behter's plea. Belgutei became close to Temüjin and later one of his generals.

Yesügei died in 1171, when Temüjin was nine. The Secret History records that he had left the boy at the home of Dai Setsen, a Khongirad noble, after the two men agreed that Temüjin and Dai Setsen's daughter Börte would marry. On the way home he came upon Tatars holding a wedding feast. He was known among them as the man who had killed their relative Temüjin Uge in a battle eight years earlier, and the boy was named after that victory. The Tatars recognised him and poisoned his food. He reached his family's camp and died three days later.

After his death Toghrul at first helped Temüjin arrange his marriage to Börte and unite the tribes, but later turned to Temüjin's anda and rival Jamukha. During the Yuan dynasty Yesügei was given the temple name Liezu, meaning Ardent Founder, and the posthumous name Shenyuan Huangdi.
yevgenia-ginzburg: Yevgenia Solomonovna Ginzburg was born in Moscow on 20 December 1904, the daughter of Solomon Natanovich Ginzburg, a Jewish pharmacist, and Revekka Markovna Ginzburg. The family moved to Kazan in 1909. In 1920 she began to study social sciences at Kazan State University, later switching to pedagogy, and she worked as a teacher at a rabfak, a workers' faculty.

In April 1934 she was confirmed as a docent, roughly an associate professor, specialising in the history of the All-Union Communist Party, and was soon named head of a new department of the history of Leninism. By the autumn of 1935 she had been forced to leave the university. Around 1930 she married Pavel Aksyonov, the mayor of Kazan; their son Vasily Aksyonov, born in 1932, became a well-known writer.

After the assassination of Sergei Mironovich Kirov on 1 December 1934, Ginzburg was accused of taking part in a counter-revolutionary Trotskyist group said to be led by Professor Nikolay Naumovich Elvov and centred on the newspaper Krasnaya Tatariia, where she worked. She was expelled on 8 February 1937 and arrested on 15 February. Unlike most of those around her, she denied the charges from the first interrogation. Her husband was arrested in July and sentenced to 15 years of corrective labour.

On 1 August 1937 a closed session of the Military College of the Supreme Court sentenced her to ten years' imprisonment. She was shipped to Magadan and sent to the camps of the Kolyma valley, where heavy general work left her emaciated. A Crimean German doctor, Anton Walter, recommended her for nursing work at Taskan, and they later married. Released from the camp system in February 1949, she was ordered to stay in Magadan and began to write her memoirs in secret. She was arrested again in October 1949 and exiled, with Kolyma as her destination at her own request.

After Stalin's death in 1953 and her repeated appeals, she was released from exile and rehabilitated on 25 June 1955. She returned to Moscow, and finished her memoir after Walter's death in 1959. It could not be published in the USSR, but the manuscript was smuggled abroad and appeared in 1967 from Mondadori in Milan and Possev in Frankfurt, and has since been translated into many languages. She died in Moscow aged 72. Marleen Gorris directed a film of her story, Within the Whirlwind, with Emily Watson in the title role.
yi-i: Yi I was born in Gangneung, Gangwon Province, in 1536 into the Deoksu Yi clan. His father, Yi Won-su, was a Left Second State Councillor, and his mother, Shin Saimdang, was an accomplished artist and calligrapher. He was the grandnephew of Yi Ki, Chief State Councilor from 1549 to 1551. He studied under Baek In-geol, successor of Cho Kwangjo, and is said to have finished his lessons in the Confucian classics by seven and passed the Civil Service literary examination at 13.

After his mother's death when he was 16 he secluded himself on Kumgang-san for three years, studying Buddhism. He left the mountains at 20 and devoted himself to Neo-Confucianism. He married at 22 and the next year visited Yi Hwang at Dosan. His father died when he was 26.

He passed special examinations with top honours with a thesis called Cheondochaek, widely regarded as a literary masterpiece that displayed his knowledge of history, Confucian political philosophy and Taoism. He took top honours in civil examinations nine times in a row. He held government posts from the age of 29, went on a mission in 1568 as a document officer, took part in writing the Myeongjong Annals, and at 34 wrote Dongho Mundap, an eleven-article political memorial arguing that righteous government could be achieved.

By about 40 he had the deep trust of the king and was one of the central political figures. When political conflicts escalated in 1576 his efforts proved fruitless and he returned home to study and teach. He came back to office at 45 and held several ministerial posts, writing works that recorded crucial events and tried to ease the conflicts of the time. King Seonjo remained noncommittal, and Yi found it hard to stay neutral. He left office in 1583 and died the following year.

Yi did not fully agree with the dualistic Neo-Confucianism of Yi Hwang. His school stressed concrete, material elements and external experience and learning rather than inner spiritual perception. Unlike Yi Hwang, who disliked politics, he was an active official who wanted Confucian principles applied to administration, with sage learning and self-cultivation as its base. He proposed raising and strengthening an army against a possible Japanese attack, but the central government rejected it, and he died before the Imjin war began.

His works include Questions and Answers at East Lake, the Memorial in Ten Thousand Words, The Essentials of the Studies of the Sages, The Secret of Expelling Ignorance and the Daily Records of Lectures before the Throne. The Complete Works of Yulgok was compiled after his death. A street in Seoul, Yulgongno, is named after him.
yi-sun-sin: Yi Sun-sin was born on 28 April 1545 in Hanseong, the present Seoul, to Yi Chŏng and a lady of the Ch'ogye Pyŏn clan. His family belonged to the Deoksu Yi clan. His grandfather had entered government service but was later impeached in the Gimyo literati purge, and his father did not pursue a government career. As a child Yi played war games and was always chosen as leader.

In 1576 Yi passed the military examination at thirty-two, after first failing when he broke a leg in the cavalry test. He was posted to the northern frontier in Hamgyeong province, defended border settlements against Jurchen raiders and became known for his strategy and leadership. In 1583 he lured the Jurchen into battle and captured their chief, Mu Pai Nai.

In 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered the invasion of Korea as a base for conquering Ming China. The Japanese landed at Busan, met no naval resistance and reached Seoul in nineteen days. Yi began naval operations from Yeosu. Though he had never commanded a naval battle, he won the Battle of Okpo, the Battle of Sacheon and several others, and is generally accepted to have fought at least 23 naval battles and won them all. At Myeongnyang he led a fleet of 13 ships against at least 133 Japanese ships. Court factionalism led ministers to portray him to King Seonjo as a potential traitor, and he was arrested and tortured, but Prime Minister Yu Sŏngnyong's defence saved him from execution twice.

Yi died of a gunshot wound on 16 December 1598 in the Battle of Noryang, the last major battle of the Imjin War. After his death he received the title Chungmugong, Duke of Loyalty and Warfare, and the posthumous office of prime minister. His wartime journals, the Nanjung Ilgi, are part of UNESCO's Memory of the World initiative. Some military historians, among them Joseph Cummins and George Alexander Ballard, place him on a par with Horatio Nelson. A shrine to him stands in Asan, where he spent his youth.
yiddish: Yiddish, historically called Judeo-German or Jewish German, is a West Germanic language that originated in the Holy Roman Empire in the Middle Ages. By the 10th century a distinctive Jewish culture had formed in Central Europe, centred on the Rhineland (Mainz) and the Palatinate (notably Worms and Speyer), an area that came to be known as Ashkenaz. Yiddish gave the nascent Ashkenazi community a vernacular based on High German, fused with many elements from Hebrew, notably Mishnaic Hebrew, and to some extent Aramaic. Most varieties also include Slavic elements. It has traditionally been written in the Hebrew alphabet, and its orthography developed towards the end of the High Middle Ages.

The earliest surviving references, from the 12th century, call the language loshn-ashknaz, the language of Ashkenaz, or taytsh, a variant of the name for Middle High German. Colloquially it is mame-loshn, the mother tongue, as against loshn koydesh, the holy tongue, meaning Hebrew. The oldest surviving literary document in Yiddish is a blessing in the Worms machzor, a Hebrew prayer book, first recorded in 1272. Eastern Yiddish, far more common today, differs from Western Yiddish, which Ethnologue classifies as endangered, by its size and its extensive Slavic vocabulary.

Printing in the 16th century allowed cheap large-scale production of Yiddish works. Elia Levita, the earliest named Yiddish author, composed the Bovo-Bukh about 1507-08, printed from 1541. From the late 18th century, under the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, the language lost prestige, stigmatised by assimilationists and later by Zionists in favour of national languages and Hebrew.

In the early 20th century, especially after the October Revolution, Yiddish emerged as a major Eastern European language, with a flourishing literature, theatre and cinema, and the Yiddish Scientific Institute, YIVO, was founded in 1925. Before the Second World War there were 11 to 13 million speakers. About 85 per cent of the approximately six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust were Yiddish speakers, and the language declined massively. It is still spoken in Haredi communities, and a 2021 estimate counted 600,000 speakers in all.
yigael-yadin: Yigael Yadin was born Yigael Sukenik in Jerusalem on 20 March 1917, when the city was part of Ottoman Palestine. His father was the Polish-Jewish archaeologist Eleazar Sukenik, and his mother, Hasya Sukenik-Feinsold, was a teacher and women's rights activist. He joined the Haganah at the age of 15. In 1946 he left it after an argument with its commander, Yitzhak Sadeh, over whether a machine gun should be standard squad equipment.

In 1948 Yadin interrupted his university studies to return to active service and was Israel's Head of Operations in the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, responsible for many of its key decisions. In April he oversaw the secret biological warfare operation Cast Thy Bread, a campaign to poison the wells of Palestinian villages with bacteria and prevent the return of the evicted, probably with David Ben-Gurion's authorisation. He became Chief of Staff of the Israel Defense Forces on 9 November 1949 and resigned on 7 December 1952 over Ben-Gurion's cuts to the military budget.

He then turned to archaeology. In 1956 he received the Israel Prize in Jewish studies for his doctoral thesis on the Dead Sea Scrolls: his father had bought three of the seven scrolls found in 1947, and Yadin bought the other four in New York in 1954. He excavated the Qumran Caves, Masada, Hazor, Tel Megiddo and caves in the Judean Desert where objects of the Bar Kokhba revolt were found, and he thought the Solomonic Gate at Tel Gezer the high point of his career.

Yadin was military adviser to Prime Minister Levi Eshkol on the eve of the Six-Day War, and after the Yom Kippur War he sat on the Agranat Commission. In 1976 he founded the Democratic Movement for Change, known as Dash, in response to alleged corruption in the Labor Alignment. In the elections of 1977 Dash won 15 of the 120 seats in the Knesset and joined Menachem Begin's coalition after a few months.

As Deputy Prime Minister he played an important part in the contacts with Egypt that led to the Camp David Accords and the peace treaty. Dash broke into splinter factions, and he sat as an independent for the rest of his term. He retired from politics in 1981, and died on 28 June 1984 of a heart attack.
yinchuan: Yinchuan lies in the middle of the Yinchuan Plain, sheltered from the deserts of Mongolia by the Helan Mountains to the west. The Yellow River runs through the area from south-west to north-east, and the plain has been irrigated by a canal system developed as long ago as the Han and Tang dynasties, which makes it very productive. The climate is a cold desert one, with about 194 mm of rain a year, dry cold winters and short hot summers.

The area was home to Shuidonggou, an early Paleolithic site more than 30,000 years old, and rock art was later made in the Helan Mountains. In the 1st century BCE the place was a county called Fuping, renamed Huaiyuan in the 6th century CE. After the fall of the Tang dynasty in 907 it came under the Tanguts, and in 1038 their leader Yuanhao declared himself emperor of the Great Xia. Many of the native Han population emigrated in response. The Pagoda of Chengtian and the Western Xia mausoleums were built in this period.

In the autumn of 1209 the Mongols besieged the city, by then called Zhongxing. A garrison of 150,000 held out, though Western Xia submitted to Mongol suzerainty. After the Xia tried to reassert its independence, the Mongols returned in 1227 and slaughtered the city's entire population; Genghis Khan died during the siege in circumstances that are debated. Under the Ming and Qing the city was the seat of the prefecture of Ningxia. In 1739 the Yinchuan–Pingluo earthquake levelled it, killing over 15,300 people.

Yinchuan became the capital of Ningxia province when it was formed from part of Gansu in 1928. In 1954 the province was abolished and the city passed to Gansu, but with the creation of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region in 1958 it became the capital again. About a quarter of its people are Hui Muslims, and most of the rest are Han Chinese. The city is the chief market for the plain's grain, wool and animal products. Among the sights are the Western Xia imperial tombs, where nine imperial tombs and 253 lesser tombs have been unearthed since 1972, and the Haibao and Chengtiansi pagodas.
yining: Yining stands on the northern side of the Ili River in the Dzungarian basin, about 70 km east of the border with Kazakhstan and about 710 km west of Ürümqi. The Ili valley is far wetter than most of Xinjiang and has rich grazing land. The city is the modern successor to the nearby ruined city of Almaliq. It is known as Ghulja in Uyghur and as Kulja in Kazakh, and in the 19th and early 20th centuries Russian and Western writers used Kulja for the whole Chinese part of the Ili basin and its two main cities.

The area was under the Chagatai Khanate from the 13th to the 15th century. Erdeni Batur, the first Khong Tayiji of the Dzungar Khanate, built a city here called Khobak Sari as the Dzungar capital, with a monastery, warehouses and settlements. Under Tsewang Rabtan and Galdan Tseren, Uyghurs were sent to farm the land and irrigation was introduced, producing wheat, barley, millet, melons, grapes, apricots and apples. Galdan Tseren built a monastery that was destroyed in the rebellion of Amursana and rebuilt in 1764 by the Qianlong emperor as the Anyuan temple.

Under the Qing the fort of Ningyuan was built in 1762 for settlers from southern Xinjiang, followed by the forts of Huining and Xichun. The Sino-Russian Treaty of Kulja of 1851 opened the area to trade. The city suffered severely in the Dungan Revolt of 1864–66. Russia seized the Ili basin in 1871, and the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881 restored it to China. A 1911 reference work distinguished Old Kulja, the commercial centre, which is today's Yining, from New Kulja or Suiding, the Chinese fortress and regional capital.

Ningyuan County was renamed Yining County in 1914 to avoid confusion with other places of that name. The East Turkestan Revolution began at Ghulja on 7 November 1944, and the city was the capital of the Second East Turkestan Republic from 12 November 1944 until 22 December 1949. Yining became a separate city from Yining County in 1952, and in 1962 major Sino-Soviet clashes took place along the Ili. It is the administrative seat of the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture and a commercial and agricultural centre of the valley, long a trading place for tea and cattle.
yinxu: Yinxu, Chinese for Ruins of Yin, lies in northern Henan, near modern Anyang and the borders Henan shares with Hebei and Shanxi. It corresponds to Yin, the final capital of the Shang dynasty. The name Yin appears not to have been used for the dynasty or its capital until the succeeding Zhou dynasty; the oracle bones call the state Shang and the capital Dayi Shang, the Great Settlement Shang. At 30 square kilometres the site is the largest archaeological site in China.

Ancient texts describe Yin as the last Shang capital but disagree on when the move took place. The Book of Documents and the Bamboo Annals say that King Pan Geng moved the capital to Yin, and the Annals add that he moved from Yan, present-day Qufu. In Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian Pan Geng instead moves it to Bo, south of the Yellow River, a location inconsistent with Yin. Yin was clearly the capital by the time of King Wu Ding, who launched numerous campaigns from it.

According to traditional accounts the last Shang king, Di Xin, was a tyrant, and Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou built support against him until the Battle of Muye ended the dynasty. The Zhou made their capital at Fenghao, and Yin was largely abandoned.

The site was then forgotten for millennia. In 1899 Wang Yirong, director of the Imperial Academy, recognised carvings on so-called dragon bones as ancient Chinese writing; by one account he found them in medicine bought for malaria. Illegal digs took tens of thousands of pieces before the source was traced to the village of Xiaotun, outside Anyang. In 1910 Luo Zhenyu identified the area as the last Shang capital. In 1917 Wang Guowei read the kings' names in the inscriptions and built a genealogy that closely matched Sima Qian's, confirming the Shang's historical authenticity.

Li Ji led the first official excavations in 1928-37, and work by the Institute of Archaeology has continued since 1950, uncovering palaces and temples, royal cemeteries, and bronze and bone workshops.

The best preserved royal tomb at Yinxu is that of Fu Hao, a military leader and wife of Wu Ding. Zheng Zhenxiang discovered it in 1976, and it has been dated to 1250 BCE. It was undisturbed and held six dog skeletons, 16 human slave skeletons and many grave goods. The tomb is open to the public, and nearby chariot pits hold the earliest animal-drawn carts found by Chinese archaeology. UNESCO selected Yinxu as a World Heritage Site in 2006.
yohannes-iv: Yohannes IV was born Kahssai Mercha. His father, Mercha Wolde Kidan, came from the ruling family of Tembien, and his mother, Silas Dimtsu, was a niece of Sabagadis Woldu, so that he descended from the ruling families of Tembien, Agame and Enderta. The first half of his life is poorly documented, and the date of his birth is given as anywhere between 1831 and 1837. He was the youngest of his siblings and is first recorded in politics during a visit to the court of Tewodros II in 1864–1865, with his brothers Gugsa and Maru.

When a British expedition marched on Magdala in 1868 to free the European captives held by Tewodros, Yohannes agreed to help its commander, Sir Robert Napier, protecting supply routes from the coast. Tewodros killed himself three days after the expedition arrived at Magdala, and British officers admitted that they could not have reached it without the help of the chiefs and people of the country. Yohannes was rewarded with ammunition and artillery.

Yohannes continued the policy of Tewodros of unifying Ethiopia. He toured each region and met the governors he appointed, usually local nobles, so long as they submitted. In his first six years he united the mainly Christian provinces, including Lasta, Semien, Begemder, Gojjam, Wollo and Shewa. He crowned Menelik King of Shewa in 1878 and Tekle Haymanot King of Gojjam in 1881, and punished both after they fought at Embabo in June 1882.

He regarded divisions in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, Islam and foreign missionaries as threats to the state. At a council at Boru Meda in 1878 supporters of one disputed doctrine who protested had their tongues cut out, and he told the Oromo chiefs of Wollo to become Christians if they wished to live in peace. It is estimated that 550,000 Oromos and Jebertis were converted by force.

Khedive Isma'il Pasha of Egypt sought to bring the whole Nile basin under his rule, and Egyptian forces occupied Harar on 11 October 1875 and entered northern Ethiopia from Massawa. Yohannes appealed to the British, then marched against them. Later, under the Hewett Treaty, he allowed Egyptian garrisons to leave the Sudan across his lands. Ras Alula defeated a Mahdist army at Kufit on 23 September 1885, but Italy took Massawa.

When Mahdist forces sacked Gondar, Yohannes marched against them and was mortally wounded at the Battle of Gallabat on 9–10 March 1889, after going beyond the lines as victory neared. He named Ras Mengesha as his son and heir before dying, but Tigray fell into rebellion, and Menelik of Shewa was proclaimed emperor as Menelik II. His descendants ruled Tigray as hereditary princes until 1974.
yom-kippur-war: The war was part of the Arab–Israeli conflict. In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel had captured the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, roughly half of Syria's Golan Heights and the West Bank. Four months before the fighting, Henry Kissinger offered Sadat's emissary Ismail an Israeli withdrawal from almost all of Sinai; Ismail never returned with a reply, and Sadat was already determined to go to war. The attack came on 6 October, the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, which coincided with the 10th day of Ramadan.

In Sinai the Egyptians deployed five divisions of 100,000 soldiers, 1,350 tanks and 2,000 guns against 450 Israeli soldiers in 16 forts along the canal. They armed their infantry with RPG-7 rockets and Sagger guided missiles, which proved devastating to the first Israeli armoured counterattacks. On the Golan the Syrians attacked with five divisions, 800 tanks and 600 artillery pieces against Israeli brigades of some 3,000 troops and 180 tanks. Dayan ordered the Jordan bridges prepared for detonation.

Arriving reserves turned the tide on the Golan from 8 October, and Israel pushed on towards Damascus. Jordan and Iraq sent forces to support Syria. In Sinai an Israeli force under Ariel Sharon crossed the Suez Canal at Deversoir, where a gap had been found between the Egyptian Second and Third Armies, and moved to encircle the Third Army. The Soviet Union airlifted 12,500 to 15,000 tons of supplies to its allies from 9 October. Resolution 338 of the Security Council demanded a ceasefire on 22 October, but fighting continued, and a second ceasefire took effect on 25 October.

After President Nixon authorised $2.2 billion in arms for Israel, Saudi Arabia declared an embargo against the United States, which led to the 1973 energy crisis. Kissinger pressed Israel not to destroy the trapped Third Army, hoping to draw Egypt away from Soviet influence. The war was a direct antecedent of the Camp David Accords of 1978 and the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty of 1979, and the last Israeli troops left Sinai on 26 April 1982.

Israel lost between 2,521 and 2,800 killed. The shock to Israelis was severe, since the army had grown complacent after 1967. Historians differ over whether the outcome was an Israeli victory, an Egyptian victory or a stalemate.
yonago: Yonago lies in the far west of Tottori Prefecture and faces the Sea of Japan to the north and Lake Nakaumi to the northwest. It adjoins Shimane Prefecture and stands across the lake from the Shimane capital of Matsue. The city limits are mostly flat, with the Hino River flowing through the Yonago Plain, while the southern part is hilly country at the foot of Mount Daisen. An irrigation canal called the Yonekawa carries water from the Hino River to Sakaiminato. The name is written with two kanji, meaning rice and child.

The area belonged to the ancient province of Hōki. According to the Kojiki, the tomb of the creator kami Izanami lies on the border of Yonago with Izumo Province, and many remains of the Yayoi and Kofun periods have been found within the city limits.

In the early Edo period the Tokugawa shogunate appointed Nakamura Kazutada daimyō of the 175,000 koku Yonago Domain, and the castle was reconstructed. The centre of the modern city grew from the castle town. After Nakamura died without an heir the domain was abolished and its lands passed to the Ikeda clan of Tottori Domain, who kept the castle and gave it to their hereditary senior retainers of the Arao clan, who ruled it until the Meiji Restoration.

The town of Yonago was established in Aioi District in October 1889, under the new system of municipalities. A post office opened in 1872, a prison in 1877 and a courthouse in 1884, and railway services began in 1902. Yonago became a city on 1 April 1927 and absorbed the neighbouring town of Yodoe on 31 March 2005.

Yonago is the second largest city of Tottori Prefecture after Tottori and the commercial centre of its western part. Most of its workforce is employed in services, and Tottori University has a campus there. Its National Historic Sites include the ruins of Yonago Castle, the Mukoeyama Kofun Cluster, the Mukibanda Yayoi remains and the Kamiyodo temple ruins. Kaike Onsen, on Miho Bay, is said to be the birthplace of the triathlon in Japan. The city is twinned with Baoding in China and Sokcho in South Korea.
yonezawa: Yonezawa lies in the southeast corner of Yamagata Prefecture and covers 548.51 square kilometres. Its southern and eastern parts are river basins surrounded by large mountains, forming the Yonezawa Basin, and the Mogami River flows through the city. The south has complex terrain of several rivers and alternating ridges and valleys running east to west. Part of the city lies within the Bandai-Asahi National Park. The climate is humid continental, with warm to hot summers, cold winters and heavy precipitation from August to October.

The area was part of ancient Dewa Province and was controlled in the Sengoku period by the Date clan. The warlord Date Masamune was born in Yonezawa. In the Edo period the area became Yonezawa Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate, ruled by the Uesugi clan. After the start of the Meiji period it was organized into Minamiokitama District, Yamagata Prefecture.

Yonezawa is best known for its local delicacies, among them apples, Yonezawa beef and carp, and as a castle town that was once home to the Uesugi clan, including the daimyō Uesugi Yozan. Its economy rests on agriculture, horticulture, light manufacturing and tourism. Local attractions include Yonezawa Castle, Tateyama Castle, the Yonezawa City Uesugi Museum, Namegawa Great Falls and the hot springs of Shirabu Onsen and Yonezawa Onsen. Yamagata University has a campus in the city. Natives include the architect Itō Chūta, the statesman Hirata Tosuke and the admirals Yamashita Gentarō and Chūichi Nagumo.
yongle-emperor: Zhu Di was born on 2 May 1360, the fourth son of Zhu Yuanzhang, who in 1368 founded the Ming dynasty as the Hongwu Emperor. On 22 April 1370 he was made Prince of Yan, with his fief at Beiping, the present Beijing, and in April 1380 he moved there. In the 1380s and 1390s he proved a skilled military leader. After the Hongwu Emperor's death, the new Jianwen Emperor's advisors set out to limit the power of the princes, removing five of them, and regarded Zhu Di as the most dangerous.

In 1399 Zhu Di rebelled in the civil war known as the Jingnan campaign. He began with 100,000 soldiers and only the area around Beiping, but his troops were of higher quality. He ascended the throne on 17 July 1402 and took the era name Yongle. He erased the Jianwen Emperor's reign from the record, and tens of thousands of people were purged, among them Huang Zicheng and Qi Tai, who were put to death with their families and followers.

He made Beiping, renamed Beijing in 1403, a second capital, and its construction between 1407 and 1420 employed hundreds of thousands of workers. He had the Grand Canal rebuilt to feed the capital and the northern armies, finishing in 1415. He sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia, which employed about two thousand scholars. Unlike his father, he avoided frequent purges. He led five campaigns into Mongolia, which failed to secure the northern border, and annexed Đại Việt in 1407 as Jiaozhi Province. In 1405 he appointed the eunuch Zheng He admiral of a fleet whose voyages reached India, Hormuz, Arabia and East Africa.

On 1 April 1424 the emperor set out on his last campaign into Mongolia, which failed. He died on 12 August 1424 at Yumuchuan, and private records suggest that a series of strokes killed him. He was buried in the Chang Mausoleum, the first of the Ming tombs north of Beijing, and his son Zhu Gaochi succeeded him as the Hongxi Emperor. Historians such as Chan Hok-lam, Edward Dreyer and Frederick Mote have described his reign as the second founding of the Ming dynasty.
yongle-encyclopedia: The Yongle Emperor, known for his military achievements, was also a reader who wished to categorize literary works into a reference encyclopedia to preserve rare books and simplify research. He raised the standing of the Hanlin Academy, which had handled clerical tasks such as drafting edicts, by selecting only top recruits and leaving clerical duties to imperial officers. In 1404, a year after the commission, a team of 100 scholars led by Xie Jin finished a manuscript called A Complete Work of Literature, but the Emperor rejected it and insisted on more volumes. In 1405 the number of scholars rose to 2,169, and they were sent across China to find books. The monk Yao Guangxiao was general editor.

The work was completed in 1408 at the Guozijian in Nanjing and filled 11,095 volumes, occupying about 40 cubic metres, with 370 million Chinese characters. It was meant to include every commentary written on the Chinese classics and all history, philosophy, arts and sciences, as a collation of excerpts and works from the whole of Chinese literature. It was handwritten, not printed, on special paper and bound in the wrapped-back style, with red ink, reserved for the emperor, for titles and authors. Entries were ordered by the sounds of characters under the Hongwu zhengyun, not by subject. Non-Confucian scholars wrote the Buddhist, Daoist and divination sections, and some Neo-Confucians dismissed the work as wheat and chaff.

The encyclopedia stood in Nanjing until 1421, when the capital moved to Beijing and it went to the Forbidden City. It narrowly escaped a fire in 1557, and the Jiajing Emperor had a manuscript copy made between 1562 and 1567. The original was lost afterwards, and theories include its burning in 1644, burial with the Jiajing Emperor, and the Qianqing Palace fire. Most of the copy was burnt or looted when Anglo-French forces invaded Beijing in 1860; about 5,000 volumes remained in 1875 and 800 by 1894, and the Boxer Rebellion and the Hanlin Academy fire cost more. The largest holding, 221 volumes, is at the National Library of China in Beijing, and the National Palace Museum in Taipei holds 62.
yongzheng-emperor: Yinzhen, the future Yongzheng Emperor, was born on 13 December 1678, the eleventh recorded son of the Kangxi Emperor and the fourth prince to survive into adulthood. His mother, a court attendant of the Manchu Uya clan, was of low status and had no right to raise her own children, so Noble Consort Tong raised him. Kangxi gave his sons a rigorous education and took them on inspection trips; Yinzhen was made a beile in 1689 and a junwang, a prince of the second rank, in 1698.

In 1712 Kangxi deposed Yinreng a second time and named no heir, which set his sons against one another. Yinzhen had supported Yinreng, built his own base of support largely out of the limelight, showed no ambition and pleaded for mercy for other princes. When Kangxi died in December 1722 Yinzhen took the throne. Kangxi's choice was known only through a testament provided by Longkodo, and no decisive evidence showed it was not fabricated, so rivals such as Yinti, Yinzhi and Yinsi opposed him.

In 1723 he adopted the era name Yongzheng, "Harmonious Justice", and it has been suggested that the second character was meant to cover his disputed claim. Much of his early reign went on purging dissidents, and he grew increasingly fearful that his brothers would plot against him.

Nian Gengyao, commander of the Qing army in Xinjiang, was demoted and forced to take poison in 1726. Immediately after his enthronement Yongzheng cracked down on corruption and debt, relying partly on a secret report system in which trusted informants wrote privately to the emperor. He made meltage fees on silver an official source of local income, grouped the merchant houses of Canton into the Cohong in 1725 and removed all foreign priests from China. When civil war tore Tibet in 1727-1728 he intervened and left a Qing Resident, the amban, and a garrison.

Yongzheng ruled for thirteen years and died suddenly in 1735, aged 56, while reading court documents. It is likely that he died of poisoning from an elixir of immortality he was taking, and his successor, the Qianlong Emperor, evicted all Taoist priests from the palace. His reign was much shorter than those of his father and his son but achieved important reforms. Many consider it authoritarian, some calling him a benevolent despot and others holding that his autocratic policies went too far.
york: York lies in the Vale of York, a flat area of fertile arable land bordered by the Pennines, the North York Moors and the Yorkshire Wolds. The city was built at the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss on a terminal moraine left by the last ice age. It grew up as a river port, and the Ouse was originally a tidal river accessible to the seagoing ships of the time. The Roman name Eburacum or Eboracum is a Latinisation of a Brittonic word that may mean place of yew trees, or alternatively property of a man named Eburos.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Mesolithic people settled in the area between 8000 and 7000 BCE. By the time of the Roman conquest the land was held by a tribe the Romans called the Brigantes, whose territory first became a client state. Its leaders later grew hostile, and the Ninth Legion was sent north of the Humber into it. The city was founded as Eboracum in 71 CE. It became the capital of Britannia Inferior, a province of the Roman Empire, and was later the capital of the kingdoms of Deira and Northumbria and of Scandinavian York.

In 1068, two years after the Norman invasion, the people of York rebelled. The rising succeeded at first, but William the Conqueror suppressed it on arriving and at once built a wooden fortress on a motte. After a second rebellion in 1069 he built another timber castle across the Ouse. Both were destroyed in 1069 and rebuilt about the time of his ravaging of Northumbria, the Harrying of the North, when he destroyed everything from York to Durham.

York declined economically in the Tudor period. The Dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII ended its monastic houses. This contributed to the Pilgrimage of Grace, an uprising of northern Catholics, and Henry restored his authority by setting up the Council of the North in the dissolved St Mary's Abbey. The railway promoter George Hudson brought the railway to York in 1839, and the city was a major railway centre by the late 19th century.

York is a cathedral city in North Yorkshire, the traditional county town of Yorkshire. Its minster, castle and city walls are all Grade I listed. The walls are the most complete in England and incorporate part of the Roman fortress wall. York Minster is a large Gothic cathedral, and the Jorvik Viking Centre and the National Railway Museum are among the city's museums.
york-minster: A bishop of York was summoned to the Council of Arles in 314, which points to a Christian community in York at that time, though archaeological evidence for Christianity in Roman York is limited. The first recorded church was a wooden structure built hurriedly in 627 to baptise Edwin, King of Northumbria. Its location and that of its successors before 1080 are unknown. It was probably in or beside the old Roman principia, the military headquarters, and so near the present minster but not directly on the same site. Excavations in 1967-73 found no remains of the churches before 1080.

A song school was founded in 627 by Paulinus of York, the first Archbishop of York, and choir schools have been associated with the minster since the 7th century. The undercroft of the present building contains re-used fabric of about 1160.

York Minster is the seat of the archbishop of York and the mother church of the diocese and province of York. It is the second-largest Gothic cathedral of northern Europe and charts the development of English Gothic architecture, with Early English transepts, a Decorated nave and chapter house, and a Perpendicular eastern arm and central tower. Most of the building dates from between 1220 and 1472, and it is built of creamy magnesian limestone quarried at Tadcaster. It has a cruciform plan, an octagonal chapter house attached to the north transept and a central tower 72 metres high.

The minster keeps most of its medieval stained glass. The Dean and Chapter commissioned John Thornton in 1405 to design the Great East Window, for which he was paid £66. Its scenes come from the Book of Revelation, and it is the largest expanse of medieval stained glass in the country. The north transept holds the Five Sisters window, five lancets of grisaille glass.

Thomas Becket's shrine at Canterbury made it a rival draw for pilgrims, and York responded by seeking a saint of its own. On 18 March 1226 Pope Honorius entered the name of William Fitzherbert, a former archbishop, among the saints. In 1279 his remains were moved to a shrine behind the high altar, and King Edward I helped carry the chest.

On 9 July 1984 a serious fire damaged the south transept, and firefighters deliberately collapsed its roof to save the rest of the building. The heat shattered the glass of the rose window, but the lead held it together so that it could be taken down and restored. The 311 panels of the Great East Window were removed for conservation in 2008, and a renovation of the east front begun in 2007 was completed in 2018. An astronomical clock installed in the north transept in 1955 commemorates airmen killed in the Second World War.
yorkshire: Yorkshire takes its name from the city of York, being York's shire.
