The name York is believed to come from the Brittonic Eburākon, probably meaning place of yew trees, which became Eboracum to the Romans, Eorfowīc to the Angles and Jórvík to the Vikings. The south-west includes Leeds, Sheffield, Bradford, Doncaster and Wakefield, and Hull lies in the south-east. The North York Moors fill the north-east, the Vale of York the centre, and the Pennines, including the Yorkshire Dales, the west. The historic boundaries were reasonably stable from 1182, when western areas went to the new county of Lancashire, until 1889.

By the late Iron Age the area was held by British Celtic tribes, the Brigantes in the north and west and the Parisi in what is now the East Riding. After the Romans left, small kingdoms arose, among them Deira in the east, Ebrauc around York and Elmet in the west. In 1066, shortly before the Battle of Hastings, Harold II marched north and defeated Tostig and Harald Hardrada of Norway at Stamford Bridge, where both were killed. Many castles, among them Richmond, Pickering, Skipton and York, were built in the Norman period.

In the Wars of the Roses, between the houses of York and Lancaster, battles were fought at Wakefield and Towton, the latter called the bloodiest ever fought on English soil. In the 16th and 17th centuries the wool textile industry moved from cottage work in the old market towns to mills in the West Riding powered by Pennine streams, helping Wakefield, Halifax, Leeds and Huddersfield to grow, while coal mining first came into prominence.

The county was divided into three ridings, East, West and North, a word of Viking origin from Threthingr, a third. Each was divided into wapentakes. York became a county corporate in 1396 and Hull in 1440, independent of the ridings. Each riding had its own lord-lieutenant from 1660, and from 1889 to 1974 the ridings were administrative counties.

Yorkshire's culture draws on Celts, Romans, Angles, Norse Vikings and Normans, and its dialect has roots in Old English and Old Norse. The white rose, once the badge of the Plantagenet House of York, is its emblem, and Yorkshire Day is observed on 1 August. York Minster is the largest Gothic cathedral in northern Europe.
yoshida-shoin: Yoshida Shōin was born Sugi Toranosuke in Hagi, in the Chōshū region, the second son of a modest-ranking samurai, Sugi Yurinosuke. At the age of four he was adopted by Yoshida Daisuke, whose house taught military studies to the daimyō, and he became heir of the Yoshida line at five when Daisuke died. His uncle Tamaki Bunnoshin hurried his education, and at eleven he impressed the daimyō Mōri Takachika with a lecture.

In 1851 he went to Edo and studied Western military science under Sakuma Shōzan, and at the end of that year he left on a four-month journey through north-eastern Japan without written permission. For this offence of dappan, fleeing the domain, he lost his samurai status and his stipend of 57 koku.

Allowed back to Edo in January 1853, Shōin saw the Black Ships of Matthew Perry at Uraga with Sakuma Shōzan and was deeply impressed by Western civilization. He first tried to board a Russian warship at Nagasaki, but it sailed early. In 1854 he followed Perry's fleet to Shimoda and, with Kaneko Shigetske, rowed a stolen fisherman's boat out to the USS Powhatan on 27 March.

He was refused and handed to the authorities. His automatic death sentence was reduced after the intervention of Kawaji Toshiakira and two senior councillors. In the Noyama Prison at Hagi he lectured fellow prisoners on the Analects and Mencius and wrote a Record of Imprisonment.

Released into house arrest in 1855, he began lecturing in a small room of the Sugi house in 1856. In 1857 he took over the Shōkasonjuku Academy, which his uncle had run. His students included Kusaka Genzui, Takasugi Shinsaku, Itō Hirobumi and Yamada Akiyoshi, and since he could not travel, he sent them round Japan as investigators. In 1858 the shogunate signed a treaty without imperial sanction. Shōin proposed seizing the senior councillor Manabe Akikatsu on his way to Kyoto, killing him if he refused to act, but most of his disciples opposed it. He was imprisoned again.

Moved to Edo during the purge directed by the Tairō Ii Naosuke, Shōin confessed to the plot before the Council of State and was sentenced to death. He was beheaded on 21 November 1859, aged 29. Of his students, Takasugi Shinsaku led rifle companies against the shogunate's army in 1864, and Itō Hirobumi became Japan's first prime minister; Katsura Kogorō, Inoue Kaoru and Yamagata Aritomo also became known. He was enshrined in Setagaya in 1882, at Hagi, and at Yasukuni Shrine in 1888.
young-italy: A few months after leaving Italy, in June 1831, Giuseppe Mazzini wrote a letter to King Charles Albert of Sardinia asking him to unite Italy and lead the nation. A month later, convinced that his appeal had not reached the king, he founded the movement at Marseille, in July 1831, while in exile. Its goal was a united Italian republic, to be won by a general insurrection in the reactionary Italian states and in the lands held by the Austrian Empire, since Mazzini believed that a popular uprising would create a unified Italy.

Its slogan was Union, Strength and Liberty. Members took nicknames from figures of the Italian Middle Ages and swore an oath to make Italy united, free, independent and republican, with every man considered equal.

The movement gathered about 60,000 members around 1833. In that year members plotting a revolt in Savoy and Piedmont were arrested and executed by the Sardinian police, and in Austria links with the movement were treated as treason, punishable by death. After a second failed revolt in Piedmont and Savoy in February 1834 it disappeared for a time, then reappeared in England in 1838.

Later insurrections in Sicily, Abruzzi, Tuscany, Lombardy-Venetia, Romagna (1841 and 1845) and Bologna (1843) failed. The short-lived Roman Republic of 1848 was crushed by a French army called in by Pope Pius IX, whom Mazzini had first hailed as a likely leader of liberal unification.

Giuseppe Garibaldi joined around 1833 after meeting Mazzini, took part in a failed revolt in Piedmont and was sentenced to death, and fled to Marseille. Young Italy became affiliated with Giovine Europa, founded in 1835, alongside similar movements such as Junges Deutschland, Młoda Polska and Giovine Svizzera. A last failed revolt against Austria in Milan in 1853 effectively ended it.

The failure of the Milan revolt of 1853 crushed hopes of a democratic Italy and favoured the Piedmontese monarchy, which achieved national unification in 1860 under Count Cavour. Young Italy inspired Mlada Bosna, an early 20th-century Serbian revolutionary movement in occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, and similar youth nationalist movements in Asian and African colonies from the mid 19th century to decolonisation.
ypres: Ypres, officially Ieper in Dutch, is a city and municipality in the province of West Flanders, Belgium. The municipality includes villages such as Boezinge, Brielen, Zillebeke and Vlamertinge and has about 34,900 inhabitants. The town is known to have been raided by the Romans in the first century BCE, is first mentioned by name in 1066, and is probably named after the river Ieperlee, on whose banks it was founded.

In the Middle Ages Ypres was a prosperous Flemish city with 40,000 people in 1200, known for its linen trade with England. As the third largest city of the County of Flanders after Ghent and Bruges, it played an important part in the textile industry, and its cloth reached Novgorod in the early 12th century. The Cloth Hall was built in the 13th century. A fire in 1241 ruined much of the old city, and during the Norwich Crusade of Bishop Henry le Despenser it was besieged from May to August 1383 until French relief forces arrived. It became the seat of a new diocese in 1561.
Forces of Louis XIV took it on 25 March 1678, and Vauban built the fortifications still visible. It passed to the Habsburgs in 1713, and the French captured it again in 1794.

In the First World War Ypres stood in the path of the German sweep into France from the north. The Germans surrounded it on three sides and bombarded it for much of the war, while British, French and allied troops made costly advances from the Ypres Salient. In the Second Battle of Ypres, which began on 22 April 1915, the Germans used poison gas for the first time on a large scale, chlorine, and mustard gas was first used near the town in autumn 1917. The Third Battle of Ypres, or Passchendaele, from 31 July to 10 November 1917, brought nearly half a million casualties to all sides for only a few miles gained. The town was all but obliterated.

After the war Ypres was rebuilt with German reparations, its main square, Cloth Hall and town hall as close to the originals as possible. Britain decided in September 1920 that the Menin Gate would be a memorial, and it was unveiled on 24 July 1927; it names Commonwealth soldiers who fell in the Salient and have no known grave. Since 1929 the Last Post has been sounded there each evening at eight o'clock, apart from the German occupation of the Second World War, when it was held at Brookwood Military Cemetery in England. The Cloth Hall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, houses the In Flanders Fields Museum, and the Cat Parade is held every three years.
yser: The Yser has a course of 78 kilometres, of which about 30 are in France. It has two official sources, at Buisscheure and Lederzele, west of Cassel in the department of Nord, and passes Bollezeele and Bambecque before entering Belgium. It then flows through Diksmuide and reaches the North Sea at Nieuwpoort by the Ganzepoot lock complex. Its basin covers 1,101 square kilometres, two thirds of it in Belgium. The name IJzer is of Celtic origin, like that of the Isar in Germany, the Jizera in Bohemia and the Isère in France, since the Celtic Menapii lived in the area before Roman times.

In the Middle Ages the land between the Yser and the coast was Veurne-Ambacht. At the end of the 16th century it came into Spanish hands, and settlements and forts were built along the river against plundering by reformers from Ostend. They largely lost their function after the fall of Ostend in 1604. After the Peace of Aachen the area around Veurne passed to France, and the Yser formed a northern border of the French realm, with fortifications such as Fort Knokke. After the Treaty of Utrecht it belonged to the Austrian Netherlands, and the river gradually lost its role as a border.

In the First World War the Yser lay on the front line, with the Belgian and German armies dug in on either side. During the Battle of the Yser in 1914 part of the polder west of the river between Nieuwpoort and Diksmuide was flooded with seawater by opening the sluices, an obstacle to the advancing German army that kept the westernmost part of Belgium free of occupation. The inundation was made at the suggestion of the investigating judge of Veurne, with the cooperation of Karel Cogge and Hendrik Geeraert. The river itself never overflowed its banks.

The Belgian army held the line for the rest of the war, and monuments such as the Yser Tower and the Death March at Diksmuide recall it. In May 1940 the French and British allies blew up the bridges and locks again.
yu-the-great: Transmitted sources agree that Yu was the son of Gun, though they differ on Gun's origins. According to Sima Qian's Shiji, Gun was a mere official and Yu's descendant line ran back through Zhuanxu to the Yellow Emperor. Gun was enfeoffed at Shiniu of Mount Wen, in modern Beichuan County, Sichuan, where Yu is said to have been born, although Shifang is also named. When Yu was a child Emperor Yao made Gun Earl of Chong, and Yu is believed to have grown up on the slopes of Mount Song. He married a woman of Mount Tu, and they had a son, Qi.

An excavated manuscript, probably of the Warring States period, tells a different legend of his birth: his mother conceived by eating Job's tears grains and bore him through her back after three years.

In Emperor Yao's reign floods plagued the Chinese heartland. Gun spent more than nine years building dikes and dams, to no effect. Yu studied the river systems, and with Hou Ji devised a system of irrigation canals that led flood water into fields, while dredging the riverbeds over thirteen years. He is said to have opened the narrow channel at Mount Longmen, known since as Yu's Gateway. Tradition says he passed his own door three times in those years without going in, and that his hands and feet were thickly calloused.

Emperor Shun, impressed by his work, passed the throne to Yu rather than to his own son. Yu is said to have declined at first and to have accepted at age 53. He founded the Xia, traditionally China's first dynasty, with a capital at Anyi. According to the Book of Documents he divided the Chinese world into nine zhou, or provinces, and cast the Nine Tripod Cauldrons from bronze received from them.

According to the Bamboo Annals, Yu ruled for forty-five years; he is said to have died of an illness at Mount Kuaiji, south of present-day Shaoxing, and to have been buried there. The Yu Mausoleum, first built in the 6th century, stands four kilometres southeast of the city, and emperors, notably Qin Shi Huang, travelled there for ceremonies.

No contemporary evidence for Yu exists, and his name first appears on vessels of the Western Zhou, about a thousand years after his traditional date. Early 20th-century scholars of the Doubting Antiquity School proposed that he began as a water god or beast. Later he was regarded as an ideal ruler, and in Taoism and Chinese folk religion as a water deity.
yuan-dynasty: The Yuan was a Mongol-led dynasty and a successor state of the Mongol Empire after its division. Genghis Khan became Great Khan in 1206, and under his son Ögedei the Mongols destroyed the Jin dynasty in 1234, conquering most of northern China. Kublai, unable to read Chinese, had Han teachers from his early years and sought the counsel of Chinese Buddhist and Confucian advisers. After Möngke Khan granted him control of the Mongol territories in China, he built schools for Confucian scholars, issued paper money and revived Chinese rituals.

In 1271 Kublai issued the Proclamation of the Dynastic Name, naming the dynasty Great Yuan and claiming succession to the Chinese dynasties from the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to the Tang. He placed Genghis Khan in the imperial records as official founder, with the temple name Taizu.

The early years were unstable. Kaidu, a grandson of Ögedei, refused to submit, and the Song dynasty remained an obstacle in the south. Kublai installed the hostage prince Wonjong as ruler of Goryeo in 1259, making it a tributary, and suppressed the revolt of Li Tan in 1262. The conquest was complete in 1279, when the Southern Song fell at the Battle of Yamen.

Succession was a lasting problem. Kublai's eldest son Zhenjin died in 1285, and Zhenjin's third son ruled as Temür Khan from 1294 to 1307. Elective kurultais were held until 1311, but after 1320 they were a formality, and real power over succession lay with empress-dowagers, guard units or high officials. The final years brought struggle, famine and bitterness among the populace. In 1368 the Ming dynasty defeated the Yuan forces, and the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau, where the Northern Yuan lasted until 1635.

The population was divided into four classes: Mongols, the Semu from western and Central Asia, the Han, mostly former subjects of the Jin, and the Nan or Southerners, subjects of the Southern Song, who stood at the bottom of the privilege ladder. The imperial examinations were not restarted until 1315. Tibetan Buddhism became the de facto state religion, and the ʼPhags-pa script, invented in 1269, was used to write Mongolian, Tibetan and Chinese. Underglaze blue and white porcelain began at Jingdezhen in the early 14th century.
yuan-shao: Yuan Shao, courtesy name Benchu, was born in Ruyang County in Runan Commandery. His family had held high positions in the Han civil service for over four generations, and he was a great-grandson of Yuan An. His birth was a source of dispute with his half-brother Yuan Shu, since his mother had been a servant of Yuan Feng; the Records of the Three Kingdoms hold instead that he was an older cousin adopted by Yuan Cheng. Yuan Shao helped save some of the partisans during the Disasters of Partisan Prohibitions, and he later served as an aide to General-in-Chief He Jin, who trusted him deeply.

After Emperor Ling died in May 189, He Jin and Yuan Shao plotted against the eunuchs, and He Jin summoned Dong Zhuo's troops to Luoyang. He Jin was assassinated on 22 September 189. Dong Zhuo then seized the capital, and when Yuan Shao opposed his plan to depose Emperor Shao he fled to Ji Province. In early 190 a coalition of regional officials, including Cao Cao and Yuan Shu, formed behind him.

Dong Zhuo moved the capital to Chang'an and burned Luoyang, but the coalition's leaders, disunited, soon went home. Yuan Shao took Ji Province from Han Fu in 191 and built a state at Ye, and in the winter of that year he defeated Gongsun Zan's cavalry at the Battle of Jieqiao using massed crossbowmen.

In 195 Ju Shou urged him to welcome Emperor Xian, but Guo Tu and Chunyu Qiong opposed it, and Cao Cao took the emperor to Xuchang instead. After destroying Gongsun Zan at Yijing in 199, Yuan Shao held the four provinces north of the Yellow River and allied with the Wuhuan tribes. In 200 he marched against Cao Cao with more than 100,000 veteran troops and many militia. At Guandu, Cao Cao burned his supply depot at Wuchao, officers including Zhang He and Gao Lan defected, and Yuan Shao fled north with hundreds of men. Cao Cao defeated him again at Cangting in 201.

Yuan Shao put down rebellions in his domain and restored order, but he died on 28 June 202 without choosing between his sons Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang. Yuan Shang took the succession with the support of Shen Pei, Pang Ji and Lady Liu, and the sons then fought each other. Cao Cao eliminated Yuan Shao's heirs and remnants by 207. After taking Ye in 204 he wept at Yuan Shao's tomb and gave the family gifts and a pension. His failure, despite his family and position, was commonly blamed on indecisiveness and his inability to heed his advisers.
yuan-shikai: Yuan Shikai was born on 16 September 1859 in Zhangying village, in Xiangcheng county, to an affluent Han family, and was the fourth of six sons. He received a traditional Confucian education, failed the imperial examinations twice, in 1876 and 1879, and entered public life through the Huai Army, in which many of his relatives served. In 1882 he went to Joseon (Korea) with troops sent by Li Hongzhang to restore order, and he distinguished himself on Wu Changqing's staff. He later commanded the Chinese forces there, trained the Korean royal guard, and after he thwarted the Kapsin Coup in 1885 was made imperial resident and supreme adviser to the Korean government.

Recalled to China in 1894, he was given the task of training the New Army the next year, which formed the basis of his Beiyang Army. He took an active part in the late Qing reforms, including the abolition of the imperial examination system. The Hundred Days' reformers accused him of betrayal for tipping off Ronglu about their plans, which brought him into Empress Dowager Cixi's favour. Appointed Viceroy of Zhili in 1902, he built the Beiyang Army into the best trained force in China. After Cixi's death the Prince Regent Zaifeng dismissed him.

After the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 the Qing court recalled him, and he became prime minister on 1 November. His army fought briefly against Sun Yat-sen's revolutionaries before negotiations began. Under the deal Sun would step aside in Yuan's favour if Yuan secured the abdication of the Qing court, and Yuan became provisional president of the Republic of China.

In 1913 Yuan's alleged part in the assassination of Song Jiaoren and the reorganisation loan affair provoked Sun Yat-sen's Second Revolution, which was crushed. He outlawed the Kuomintang, dissolved the National Assembly and replaced the provisional constitution. In December 1915 he proclaimed himself Hongxian Emperor, which provoked the National Protection War. Faced with widespread opposition he abdicated in March 1916 and restored the Republic, having been emperor for only 83 days. He died of kidney failure on 6 June 1916, aged 56, leaving a weakened Beiyang government and a fragmented political landscape that soon fell into warlordism.
yucatan-peninsula: The peninsula covers approximately 181,000 km2 and has low relief, composed almost entirely of porous limestone. It is the exposed part of the larger Yucatán Platform, a flat karst landscape on the Maya Block, the southernmost part of the North American plate. It lies east of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, which some regard as the geographic boundary of Central America. The Yucatán Channel, between its north-eastern corner and Cuba, connects the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea.

The northern half has no rivers above ground. A freshwater lens floats on saline water beneath the whole peninsula, and the thousands of sinkholes called cenotes give access to it; ancient and contemporary Maya have long relied on them. The climate is tropical, semi-arid in the north-west and humid in the south, and the peninsula lies within the Atlantic hurricane belt.

The peninsula is the site of the Chicxulub crater, made 66 million years ago by an asteroid about 10 to 15 km across at the end of the Cretaceous. A ring of cenotes outlines one of the shock waves of the impact. The earliest human remains are from caves near Tulum: in 2020 divers and archaeologists excavated Chan Hol cave and found the skeleton of a woman about 30 years old who lived at least 9,900 years ago.

The peninsula makes up a large part of the ancient Maya lowlands and was a central location of Maya civilisation. Among its better-known sites are Chichen Itza, Coba, Tulum and Uxmal. In the 9th century a widespread political collapse in the central Maya region brought civil wars, the abandonment of cities and a northward shift of population, and in the Postclassic period Chichen Itza rose in the north.

The Spanish conquest of the Maya was prolonged, since the Maya kingdoms resisted integration into the Spanish Empire so tenaciously that their defeat took almost two centuries. The Caste War of Yucatán, which began in the 1840s, drove all non-natives from the region, and the independent Maya state of Chan Santa Cruz was conquered by the Mexican federal army in 1901.

The peninsula comprises the Mexican states of Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo, Guatemala's Petén Department and almost all of Belize. Maya and Mestizos make up a sizable part of the population, and Mayan languages are widely spoken. The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System stretches over 1,100 km along its eastern coast. Cattle ranching, logging, chicle and henequen were once its main products, and since the 1970s tourism has grown, above all in Quintana Roo.
yudhishthira: His name means one who is steady in battle, and he is also called Dharmaputra and Dharmaraja. According to the Mahabharata, he was born by niyoga, since a curse had made intimacy fatal for King Pandu. Pandu died in the forest and his second wife Madri ended her life, and forest sages took Kunti and the children to Hastinapura, where they were handed to Bhishma. The brothers trained under Kripa and later Drona, and Yudhishthira excelled in chariot warfare. When Duryodhana drugged and threw Bhima into the river, Yudhishthira advised his brothers to keep the matter secret and not seek revenge.

Dhritarashtra gave the Pandavas half the kingdom, the forest of Khandavaprastha, which Yudhishthira with Krishna's blessing and Vyasa's help made into the capital Indraprastha. Narada advised that Draupadi spend a year with each brother in turn, and Yudhishthira put this rule in place. For the rajasuya, Krishna suggested removing Jarasandha of Magadha, and Yudhishthira sent his brothers in four directions to subdue rival kings and gather tribute. He accepted the dice match citing the duty of a kshatriya to accept a challenge, obedience to elders and the inevitability of fate.

In exile he received from the sun god Surya the Akshaya Patra, a copper plate whose food did not run out. At a lake, a Yaksha put questions to the brothers, and the four who drank without answering died. Yudhishthira answered, and when offered one brother he chose Nakula, saying Kunti's line would live through himself and Madri's should not end, whereupon the Yaksha revived all of them. In the last year he served King Virata of Matsya in disguise as a Brahmin named Kanka. After the war he did not wish to rule, but his brothers and Bhishma persuaded him, and he reigned for 36 years and performed the Ashvamedha.

At the onset of the Kali Yuga and Krishna's departure, Yudhishthira and his brothers gave up the throne to Parikshit, Arjuna's grandson, and set out with a dog on a pilgrimage to the Himalayas towards Mount Meru. Draupadi and then each brother fell dead on the way. Yudhishthira alone ascended to heaven in his mortal body. Buddhist sources, by contrast, describe Kuru as a minor state ruled by a chieftain called Koravya of the Yuddhitthila clan.
yue-fei: Several sources state that Yue Fei was born into a poor tenant farmer's family in Tangyin County in Henan. His biography, written about sixty years after his death by his grandson Yue Ke, says that he was named Fei, meaning to fly, because a large bird like a swan landed on the roof of the house when he was born. Some later historians doubt many of Yue Ke's claims. The biography also says that he learned archery from Zhou Tong. He loved to read military classics, among them the Zuo Zhuan and the strategies of Sun Tzu and Wu Qi.

Although his literacy would have allowed him to become a scholar, he chose the military because his family had no tradition of civil service. He joined the Song army in 1122, left briefly when his father died in 1123 and returned in 1126.

After re-enlisting, Yue fought rebellious local warlords responsible for looting in northern China. He took part in defending Kaifeng during the second Jin siege in 1127. After Kaifeng fell he joined an army at Jiankang that stopped the Jurchens reaching the Yangtze in 1129. In 1133 he became general of the largest army near the central Yangtze. Between 1134 and 1135 he led a counteroffensive against Qi, a puppet state supported by the Jin, and secured territory the Jurchens had conquered.

Just as Yue threatened to retake Kaifeng, officials advised Emperor Gaozong to recall him and sue for peace. Gaozong feared that a defeat at Kaifeng might lead the Jurchen to release Emperor Qinzong, threatening his claim to the throne, and sent twelve gold plaques ordering Yue back. Yue submitted, was imprisoned, and Qin Hui arranged his execution on false charges. He died on 28 January 1142. According to his biography he tore open his jacket in court to show four characters tattooed on his back meaning serve the country with the utmost loyalty.

Yue was pardoned posthumously. Emperor Xiaozong gave him the posthumous name Wumu in 1169, and later he was made King of E. His stature as a national hero rose after his execution, strengthened in the Yuan dynasty, and temples to him were built in the Ming. Later historians blamed Qin Hui and in some accounts Gaozong. The claim that Qin Hui conspired with the Jin has never been proven. Modern accounts note that he was not the only general against the Jurchens and was not an erudite Confucian scholar, and that many exaggerations trace to Yue Ke's biography.
yuezhi: The Yuezhi are first described in Chinese histories as nomadic pastoralists living in an arid grassland in the western part of modern Gansu during the 1st millennium BCE. The Guanzi mentions nomads called the Yuzhi or Niuzhi who supplied jade to the Chinese and, unlike the neighbouring Xiongnu, did not fight nearby Chinese states. The Book of Han says the Great Yuezhi were a nomadic horde with over a hundred thousand soldiers who lived between Dunhuang and Qilian. No archaeological remains of them have been found there, and some scholars place their homeland further northwest, north of the Tian Shan. Many scholars believe they were an Indo-European people, though there is no evidence linking them to the Tarim mummies or the Tocharian languages.

After a major defeat by the Xiongnu in 176 BCE the Yuezhi split into two groups. The Lesser Yuezhi moved to the southern mountains to live with the Qiang. The Greater Yuezhi began migrating north-west about 165 BCE and settled in the Ili valley, where they defeated the Sai. In 132 BCE the Wusun, allied with the Xiongnu, dislodged them, and they passed through Dayuan in Ferghana and settled on the northern bank of the Oxus in northern Bactria.

A Chinese mission led by Zhang Qian reached them in 126 BCE to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu, but they refused, since they now lived peacefully and had no interest in revenge. Later Chinese accounts describe them as occupying Bactria in five major tribes, one of which, the Guishuang, took control of the confederation.

The Kushanas, widely believed to have been a dynastic clan or tribe of the Yuezhi, founded the Kushan Empire. At its peak, in the 3rd century CE, it stretched from Turfan in the Tarim Basin to Pataliputra on the Gangetic plain. The Kushans played an important role in the Silk Road trade and in the introduction of Buddhism to China. The Yuezhi in Bactria became Hellenized to some degree, adopting the Greek alphabet and minting coins in Greek. The Lesser Yuezhi are linked to the Yicong Hu, who helped drive the Liangzhou Rebellion of 184-221 CE, and, controversially, to the Lushui Hu, who founded the Northern Liang in 397.
yugoslav-partisans: The Kingdom of Yugoslavia was invaded from all sides on 6 April 1941, chiefly by German forces but also by Italian, Hungarian and Bulgarian formations, and the Royal Yugoslav Army surrendered unconditionally on 17 April. The leadership of the Communist Party, with Josip Broz Tito, was then in Zagreb. While the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact was in force the communists avoided open conflict with the new regime of the Independent State of Croatia, extending their underground network and gathering weapons. In June 1941 the Central Committee decided to prepare an uprising. They were the military arm of a coalition led by the Communist Party and represented by the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia, known as AVNOJ.

After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941 the Partisans began an active guerrilla campaign, and a Communist Party proclamation of 5 July called on the Serbian people to fight. A large uprising followed, later joined by the Chetniks of Draža Mihailović, and it produced the short-lived Republic of Užice, the first liberated territory in Europe. German forces suppressed the uprising by 29 November 1941. The Partisans were nonetheless a highly mobile force that the Axis offensives failed to destroy. Their stated aims were to free Yugoslav lands from the occupiers and to establish a communist-ruled state, and the Communist Party tried to appeal to the country's ethnic groups by preserving the rights of each.

Until British supplies arrived in quantity in 1944 the occupiers were their main source of arms. By late 1943 the Allies had shifted support from Mihailović to Tito as Chetnik collaboration became evident, and the Partisans were recognised at the Tehran Conference. By late 1944 they numbered about 650,000, organised in four field armies and 52 divisions, and in the autumn they and the Soviet Red Army liberated Belgrade in the Belgrade Offensive. They were also the only resistance movement in occupied Europe to use significant air and naval forces.

By the end of the war the Partisans controlled the whole country, as well as Trieste and Carinthia. After it they were reorganised as the regular armed force of the newly established Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia. Within Croatia the movement's leaders later founded the Federal Republic of Croatia as a constituent of the new federation.
yugoslavia: The idea of a common state for all South Slavic peoples emerged in the late 17th century and gained prominence through the Illyrian Movement of the 19th century. The name combines the Slavic words jug, south, and Slaveni, Slavs. After the 1917 Corfu Declaration between the Yugoslav Committee and the government of the Kingdom of Serbia, the Kingdom of Serbia merged in 1918 with the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, after centuries of foreign rule under the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy. The kingdom gained international recognition on 13 July 1922 and was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929.

On 6 January 1929 King Alexander I abolished the constitution, banned national political parties and assumed executive power; he was assassinated in 1934, and Prince Paul acted as regent. Paul signed the Tripartite Pact on 25 March 1941, and army officers overthrew him two days later, giving the 17-year-old King Peter full powers. German, Italian and Hungarian forces invaded on 6 April 1941, and the Axis powers split the country up. The Independent State of Croatia, ruled by the fascist Ustaše, persecuted and murdered around 300,000 Serbs, along with at least 30,000 Jews and Roma.

The Communist-led Partisans proclaimed a Democratic Federal Yugoslavia, and on 29 November 1945 the Constituent Assembly proclaimed a federal republic, abolishing the monarchy. Josip Broz Tito ruled from 1944 until his death on 4 May 1980. He broke with Stalin in 1948 and in 1961 helped found the Non-Aligned Movement. The country took the name Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 7 April 1963, with six republics and the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina within Serbia.

After Tito's death ethnic tensions grew. Croatia and Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991, Macedonia in September 1991, and Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence was recognised in April 1992. Wars followed, notably in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war lasted more than three years and ended with the Dayton Agreement of 14 December 1995. Serbia and Montenegro formed a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April 1992, renamed Serbia and Montenegro in 2003, and Montenegro became independent in June 2006. Serbo-Croatian has since diverged into four standard varieties, Bosnian, Croatian, Montenegrin and Serbian, and some people from the former Yugoslavia still describe themselves as Yugoslavs.
yugurs: The Yugurs, traditionally known as Yellow Uyghurs, are a Turko-Mongol people and one of the 56 ethnic groups officially recognised in China. Their own names are Sarığ yoğır in the western group and Shera yogor in the eastern. The 2020 census counted 14,706 of them, living mainly in the Sunan Yugur Autonomous County in Gansu. The Turkic-speaking Yugurs are considered descendants of a group of Old Uyghurs who fled south from Mongolia to Gansu after the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed in 840.

In Gansu those Uyghurs established the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, which lasted from 870 to 1036, with its capital near Zhangye, at the foot of the Qilian Mountains in the valley of the Ejin River. In 1037 the Yugurs came under Tangut rule. After Khizr Khoja's invasion of Qumul, residents who rejected conversion to Islam fled to nearby Dunhuang and Hunan in China proper, and these are regarded as the ancestors of the Yugurs, who have remained Vajrayana Buddhists to the present day.

In the late 16th century they adopted the Gelug order of Tibetan Buddhism under the influence of Sonam Gyatso, the third Dalai Lama. In 1893 the Russian explorer Grigory Potanin, the first Western scientist to study them, published a small glossary of Yugur words with notes on their administration and geography.

The Yugurs speak two languages of different families. About 4,600 speak Western Yugur, a Siberian Turkic language that has preserved many archaisms of Old Uyghur, and about 2,800 speak Eastern Yugur, a Mongolic language. Mongolic and Chinese are also used in the eastern provinces. Both Yugur languages are now unwritten, although the Old Uyghur alphabet remained in use in some Yugur communities until the end of the 17th century. Most Yugurs are Tibetan Buddhists.
yumjaagiin-tsedenbal: Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal, born Tserenpil, was born on 17 September 1916 to an unwed Dörbet mother in a banner of what is now Uvs Province. In October 1929 he and 21 other Mongolian students were chosen for a special preparatory school in Irkutsk in the Soviet Union, and in 1931 he joined the Mongolian Revolutionary Youth League. He graduated from the Siberian Financial and Economic Institute in July 1938, was noticed by the Soviet Communist Party's Central Committee on a visit to Moscow, and returned to Mongolia that September.

Recommended to the leader Khorloogiin Choibalsan by a Soviet intelligence officer, Tsedenbal joined the party in 1939 and became finance minister. In March 1940, aged 24, he was elected general secretary, the country's number-two leader, after Choibalsan had the sitting secretary Banzarjavyn Baasanjav purged; Baasanjav was executed and rehabilitated in 1957. Tsedenbal introduced the Cyrillic script for Mongolian. After Choibalsan died in January 1952 he became premier on 27 May, and in 1958 he ousted Dashiin Damba, who had held the party post since 1954, and exiled him internally.

He resisted de-Stalinization: he blocked the commission re-examining the purges, banned the film Tümnii Neg in 1963, and a statue of Stalin stood before the National Library until 1990. He expelled rivals on charges of nationalism, among them Daramyn Tömör-Ochir in 1962, after the planned celebration of Genghis Khan's 800th anniversary was cancelled, and in 1964 an "anti-party group" of three economic officials. He called the Soviet relationship one of elder and younger brother, sided with the USSR in the Sino-Soviet split, and signed a treaty in 1966 that allowed Soviet troops to be stationed in Mongolia. He built a cult of personality, awarding himself the rank of marshal in 1979.

Memory loss and dizziness troubled him from late 1973. He resigned as premier in 1974, becoming head of state. In November 1983 the new Soviet leadership judged his behaviour a liability, and on 23 August 1984 the Mongolian Politburo dismissed him from all positions, citing his health. He lived in retirement in Moscow, where he died on 20 April 1991.

In 1988 the official media began blaming him by name for the country's stagnation, and in March 1990, at the height of the democratic revolution, the party stripped him of his titles and expelled him. A decree of President Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat in 1997 invalidated that decision. A statue of him was built in 2000, and his legacy, controversial after 1990, is remembered in Mongolia as one of relatively moderate socialism.
yungang-grottoes: The grottoes were formerly known as the Wuzhoushan Grottoes. After the decline of the Western Jin the northern parts of China came under the Tuoba-ruled Northern Wei, who made the city of Pingcheng, now Datong, their capital, and construction there increased. The Northern Wei adopted Buddhism early as their state religion. It reached the area by the North Silk Road, the northernmost route, about 2,600 km long, which connected Chang'an to the west by the Wushao Ling Pass to Wuwei and emerged at Kashgar before linking to ancient Parthia.

The site lies about 16 km west of Datong, in the valley of the Shi Li river at the base of the Wuzhou Shan mountains. The caves were excavated in the south face of a sandstone cliff about 2,600 feet long and 30 to 60 feet high. There are 53 major caves, 51,000 niches housing as many Buddha statues, and around 1,100 minor caves. The first period of carving lasted until 465, and these caves are now numbered 16 to 20. From about 471 a second phase lasted until 494, when the twin caves 5/6, 7/8 and 9/10, and caves 11, 12 and probably 13, were made under the supervision and support of the imperial court.

Imperial patronage ended in 494 when the Wei court moved to the new capital of Luoyang. The other caves were made under private patronage until 525, when uprisings in the area brought construction to a final halt.

Cave 6 is one of the richest, with a surface area of about 1,000 square metres. Its whole interior is carved and painted, and a stupa pillar in the centre rises from floor to ceiling. The upper walls carry standing Buddhas, Bodhisattvas and monks among celestial figures. The caves have been repainted as many as twelve times, so the original scheme is hard to determine.

Yungang is one of the three principal ancient Buddhist sculptural sites of China, with Longmen and Mogao. The exposed sandstone has weathered heavily since construction ended. In the Liao dynasty some statues were renewed, and the ten temples of Yungang, built from 1049 to 1060 to protect the main caves, were destroyed by fire some sixty years later. The wooden buildings in front of caves 5 and 6 date from 1621, in the late Ming.

Red Guards damaged many carvings during the Cultural Revolution, and bullet marks are still visible. Since the 1950s cracks in the sandstone have been sealed by grouting. UNESCO made the grottoes a World Heritage Site in 2001, calling them a masterpiece of early Chinese Buddhist cave art that represents the fusion of Buddhist symbolic art from south and central Asia with Chinese cultural traditions.
yunnan: Yunnan is the most south-western province of China, with the Tropic of Cancer running through its southern part. It covers about 394,000 km2, 4.1 percent of the country's area. The north belongs to the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, with a canyon region in the west and a plateau region in the east. It shares a border of 4,060 km with Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam, holds nine lakes of more than 30 km2, among them Dianchi near Kunming and Erhai near Dali, and is China's most biologically diverse province.

The Yuanmou Man, a Homo erectus fossil, is dated to about 1.7 million years ago. Around the 3rd century BCE the area near present-day Kunming was known as Dian, and the Chu general Zhuang Qiao set himself up as King of Dian. The Han dynasty conquered Dian in 109 BCE and founded the Yizhou commandery. In the 320s CE the Cuan clan migrated in, and ruled eastern Yunnan for over four hundred years. Around Lake Erhai six local regimes called zhao emerged; the southernmost, Mengshe, became Nanzhao, which lasted from 738 to 937.

In 937 Duan Siping founded the Dali Kingdom, which the Mongol Empire conquered in 1253 after King Duan Xingzhi defected. In 1273 Kublai Khan appointed Ajall Shams al-Din Omar as governor. The Ming dynasty destroyed the Yuan loyalists and the remnants of the House of Duan by the early 1380s and installed Mu Ying and his family as hereditary aristocrats. Under the Ming and Qing large areas were run under the native chieftain system. After 1911 local warlords governed with unusual autonomy, financing themselves through opium.

Yunnan has about 47 million people, and its capital is Kunming. From the Yuan dynasty two major waves of migration from Han-majority areas reached the province. Ethnic minorities make up about 34 percent of the population; the main groups are the Yi, Bai, Hani, Zhuang, Dai and Miao. Yunnan has been identified as the birthplace of tea.
yuri-dolgoruky: Yuri was the sixth son of Vladimir Monomakh and a prince of the Monomakhovichi branch of the ruling house. It is unclear when he was born. Some chronicles quote his elder brother Viacheslav, born in 1083, as saying he was already bearded when Yuri was born, which would put the birth around 1099 or 1100, but the Primary Chronicle records Yuri's first marriage on 12 January 1108, which implies an earlier date. His first wife was a daughter of Ayyub Khan, a Cuman khan. His second wife was Helena, who survived him and moved to Constantinople. He had at least fifteen children, among them Andrei Bogolyubsky and Vsevolod the Big Nest.

In 1108 Vladimir Monomakh sent Yuri to govern the Vladimir-Suzdal principality in the north-east of Kievan Rus' in his name. In 1121 he quarrelled with the boyars of Rostov and moved his capital to Suzdal. The area was sparsely populated, and he founded many fortresses and towns, among them Ksniatin in 1134, Pereslavl-Zalesski and Yuriev-Polski in 1152 and Dmitrov in 1154. In 1147 he met Sviatoslav Olgovich in a place called Moscow, and in 1156 he fortified Moscow with wooden walls and a moat. The settlement probably existed earlier or later than that, but Yuri is often called its founder.

He also coveted the throne of Kiev. After the death of his brother Mstislav of Kiev in 1132, when the Rus lands fell apart in the words of a chronicle, he declared war on the princes of Chernigov, put his son on the throne of Novgorod and seized Pereyaslav of the South. The Novgorodians betrayed him, and he took revenge by seizing Torzhok. He captured Kiev in 1149 but was driven out in 1151 by his nephew Iziaslav, and regained it in 1155.

Yuri died in 1157, presumably poisoned at the feast of a Kievan nobleman, and his death set off an anti-Suzdalian uprising in Kiev. He was interred at the Saviour Church in Berestovo, though his tomb is empty. His autocratic rule and perceived foreign status had made him unpopular with the Kievan boyars. His reign is seen as marking the effective end of the unified Rus' until the Mongol invasions, as powerful provincial territories such as Vladimir-Suzdal and Galicia-Volhynia competed for the throne of Kiev. A monument to him designed by Sergei Orlov was erected on Tverskaya Street in Moscow in 1954.
yuri-gagarin: Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was born on 9 March 1934 in the village of Klushino, in the Russian SFSR, the third of four children of a carpenter and a dairy farmer who worked on a sovkhoz. The Germans captured Klushino on 18 October 1941, burned down the school and 27 houses and forced the residents to work the farms. The Gagarins spent 21 months in a mud hut behind their house until the occupation ended, and in early 1943 his two elder siblings were deported to Poland for slave labour.

In 1950, aged 16, he began an apprenticeship as a foundryman at a steel plant in Lyubertsy, near Moscow. He then studied tractors at the Industrial Technical School in Saratov, where he volunteered at a local flying club. In 1955 he was accepted to the First Chkalov Higher Air Force Pilots School in Orenburg, and on 5 November 1957 he was commissioned a lieutenant in the Soviet Air Forces.

After the launch of Luna 3 in October 1959 he expressed interest in space exploration. Sergei Korolev, the chief engineer of the Vostok programme, specified that candidates should weigh under 72 kg and be no taller than 1.70 metres to fit the capsule; Gagarin was 1.57 metres tall. He was among the first twelve cosmonauts approved on 7 March 1960.

On 12 April 1961, travelling on Vostok 1 and launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome, he completed one orbit of the Earth in 108 minutes and became the first person in space. Nikita Khrushchev awarded him the title Hero of the Soviet Union. He toured widely abroad, accepting invitations from about 30 countries. Vostok 1 was his only spaceflight: he was backup crew to Soyuz 1, in which his friend Vladimir Komarov was killed, and Soviet officials then banned him from further flights.

On 27 March 1968, on a routine training flight, Gagarin and the flight instructor Vladimir Seryogin died when their MiG-15UTI crashed near the town of Kirzhach. Their ashes were interred in the Kremlin wall. The cause of the crash is uncertain. At least three investigations were held, and a KGB report declassified in March 2003 blamed out-of-date weather information and external fuel tanks left on the aircraft.

The date of his flight, 12 April, has been marked as Cosmonautics Day since 1962 in the Soviet Union and since 1991 in Russia and some other former Soviet republics. In 2011 the United Nations declared it the International Day of Human Space Flight.
yury-of-moscow: Yury Danilovich was the eldest son of Daniel of Moscow, the first prince of Moscow. His first military action was the defence of Pereslavl-Zalessky against Andrey of Gorodets, grand prince of Vladimir. Because Daniel had never held the grand princely title, his descendants had no legitimate claim to Vladimir under the traditional rules of succession. When Andrey died on 27 July 1304, Tokhta, khan of the Golden Horde, therefore gave the title to Yury's uncle, Mikhail of Tver. Yury rebelled, and two campaigns by Mikhail against Moscow, in 1305 and 1308, forced him to accept the khan's decision.

Yury meanwhile arranged the murder of Prince Konstantin of Ryazan, whom his father had captured in 1302 and held in Moscow, and annexed the Ryazan fortress of Kolomna. He also took Mozhaisk, which had belonged to the princes of Smolensk. By 1314 he had the backing of Metropolitan Peter and a military alliance with Novgorod against Tver.

In 1315 he went to the Horde, where he spent two years. His bride Konchaka converted to Orthodox Christianity and was baptised Agafiia. Returning with a large force of Tatars, he approached Tver, but his army was defeated and his wife and his brother Boris were captured; he fled to Novgorod and sued for peace. When his wife died unexpectedly as a hostage in Tver, he told the khan that Mikhail had ordered her poisoned. Both princes were summoned to Sarai, and after a trial Mikhail was executed on 22 November 1318.

As grand prince from 1318 to 1322 Yury was resisted by other princes and by the people, who thought his appointment illegitimate. He was charged with gathering the tribute for the Horde, and in his last two years in the office the khan sent no fewer than four punitive expeditions to the northeastern principalities to enforce it.

In 1322 Dmitry of Tver persuaded the khan at Sarai that Yury had kept a large part of the tribute, and received the patent for Vladimir himself. Yury then led the army of Novgorod against the Swedes, founded a fort at the mouth of the Neva River, signed the Treaty of Orekhovo in 1323 and conquered Velikiy Ustyug the same year. Summoned to the Horde for trial, he was killed by Dmitry on 21 November 1325 before any formal investigation. Dmitry was executed at the Horde eight months later. Early in 1326 Yury's remains were brought to Moscow and buried by the bishops under Metropolitan Peter.
yushu-tibetan-autonomous-prefecture: Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture covers 188,794 square kilometres in the south-west of Qinghai Province and is largely inhabited by Tibetans. It is also transliterated Yüxü or Yulshul. Its seat is the town of Gyêgu in Yushu County, the place of the old Tibetan trade mart of Jyekundo, and the official source of the Yellow River lies within it. Historically the area belongs to the cultural realm of Kham in eastern Tibet.

Almost all of the prefecture lies in the uppermost basins of three of Asia's great rivers, the Yellow River, the Yangtze and the Mekong, and a large part of it forms the Sanjiangyuan National Nature Reserve, which protects their headwaters. Most people live in the south-east, in the valleys of the upper Yangtze, known in Chinese as the Tongtian River and in Tibetan as Drichu, and of the Mekong, the Dzachu. The highlands and the west have very little population. Elevations are above 3,600 metres, with long, cold winters and short, rainy summers, and most rain falls from June to September.

The area is rich in Tibetan Buddhist monasteries. As part of the former kingdom of Nangchen, it was for most of its history not under the domination of the Dalai Lama's Gelugpa order in Lhasa, and this different balance of power allowed the older Tibetan Buddhist orders to prevail. Of 195 lamaseries before 1958 only 23 belonged to the Gelugpa. More than 100 followed the Kagyupa schools, some of whose sub-sects are found only in this part of Tibet. The Sakyapa had 32 monasteries, many of them among the most significant in Kham, and the Nyingmapa had about as many. The Bönpo had only one, shared with the Nyingmapa.

Before collectivisation in 1958 the monastic population of the present prefecture exceeded 25,000 monks and nuns, among them about 300 incarnate lamas. On average three to five per cent of the people were monastic, and in Nangchen county the share was between 12 and 20 per cent.

The prefecture is divided into five counties and one county-level city. Its produce includes wheat, millet and black highland barley. The eastern part is served by China National Highway 214 and by Yushu Batang Airport, which opened in 2009, and in 2017 the G0613 Xining–Lijiang Expressway was completed. On 14 April 2010 an earthquake struck the prefecture at 07:49 local time, with a magnitude of 6.9 according to the USGS and EMSC and 7.1 according to Xinhua.
yusuf-adil-shah: Yusuf was born in 1450, and accounts of his origin differ. He may have been a Georgian slave purchased by Mahmud Gawan, the Bahmani prime minister; other historians call him Persian or Turkmen, and one theory makes him a Turkman of the Aq-Quyunlu. The historian Firishta presents him as a son of the Ottoman sultan Murad II, a story that modern historians consider unfounded. The Portuguese knew him as Hidalcão.

He rose quickly in the Bahmani sultan's favour and was made governor of Daulatabad; Mahmood Shah Bahmani II gave him the title Adil Khan. He led the foreigners, the Afaqis, in their conflict with the local nobility, the Deccanis, a struggle in which Mahmud Gawan was put to death in 1481. Yusuf then left Daulatabad to seize Gawan's former territories of Bijapur and Belgaum, and soon came into conflict with Malik Naib, leader of the Deccani party.

He and his son Ismail did not place the title Shah before their names but kept Adil Khan, out of respect for the Bahmanis; Ibrahim Adil Shah I formally claimed independence in 1538 and was the first of the line to use it. At Bijapur Yusuf built the citadel, the Arkilla, and the palace called the Faroukh Mahal. He invited poets and artisans from Persia, Turkey and Rome to his court and was himself an accomplished musician and scholar.

He was killed in the Battle of Koilkonda against Vijayanagara on 5 December 1510, a few days after the loss of Goa. His son Ismail Adil Shah, a minor, succeeded him, aided in his rule by a certain Kamal Khan. Yusuf had married Punji, sister of the Maratha lord Mukundrao Kadam, who was renamed Bubuji Khanum; their daughters married the sultans of Ahmednagar and Berar and a Bahmani prince. The sultanate he founded lasted for close to two centuries, until Aurangzeb ended it in 1686.
yusuf-balasaguni: Yusuf Khass Hajib was a Turkic poet, statesman, vizier and philosopher, described as a Maturidi theologian, from Balasagun, the capital of the Kara-Khanid Khanate in what is now Kyrgyzstan. Most of what is known about him comes from his own writings in the Kutadgu Bilig. He is usually called Yusuf Balasaguni after his city. Balasagun lay at the Burana archaeological site near the present-day city of Tokmok in northern Kyrgyzstan. His birth is estimated at 1018 or 1019. His father was one of the prominent and wealthy people of the time, and the young poet received his first education in his home town.

Yusuf began the Kutadgu Bilig, meaning Blessed Knowledge or Wisdom of Royal Glory, in Balasagun and finished it in Kashgar at the age of 54, in either 1069 or 1070. He wrote in the Turkic language of the Kara-Khanid era. It was the first work written in the language of the Muslim Turks, and many Turkic-speaking peoples regard it as the source and first masterpiece of their written literature of the Muslim era. In its opening lines the poet notes that the Arabs and Tajiks have many books, and that in his own language this work is only a beginning.

After he presented the finished work to Hasan ibn Sulayman, the Kara-Khanid prince of Kashgar and father of Ali-Tegin, he was awarded the title Khass Hajib, an honorific like Privy Chamberlain or Chancellor. Some scholars suspect that the prologue, which is much more openly Islamic than the rest of the text, was not written by Yusuf. This is above all true of the first prologue, which is in prose, unlike the remainder.

The date and place of his death are not recorded in any direct source. One tradition holds that he died at 55 and was buried in the south of Kashgar. His mausoleum at Tainap, Kashgar, was built in 1865 by Yakub Beg of Yettishar, destroyed in 1972 during the Cultural Revolution, and replaced by a school. After the death of Mao Zedong the mausoleum was restored on its site and the school moved. Several unknown burials were found during the work. The grave is decorated with inscriptions in Chinese, Arabic and Uyghur.

Kyrgyz National University was named after him in 2002, and a monument to him stands in Bishkek. His portrait appears on the Kyrgyz banknote of 1000 soms, and the National Bank of Kyrgyzstan issued commemorative coins for the thousand years since his birth. Streets in Kyrgyzstan, and in Tashkent, Andijan and Samarkand, bear his name, and the International Organization of Turkic Culture declared 2016 the Year of Yusuf Khass Hajib.
yusuf-ibn-tashfin: Yusuf was a Berber of the Banu Turgut, a branch of the Lamtuna, a tribe of the Sanhaja confederation. Abu Bakr ibn Umar led the Lamtuna as chief commander after his brother Yahya was killed in 1056, took Sous and its capital Aghmat, and entrusted his cousin Yusuf with Sous and the northern provinces. Yusuf's standing grew so far that Abu Bakr gave him his wife, Zaynab an-Nafzawiyyah, and judged recapture of the post politically unfeasible. In 1061 Yusuf took the title Amir al-Muslimin, recognising the Abbasid caliph as Amir al-Mu'minin.

Yusuf built an army of Sudanese contingents, Christian mercenaries and Saharan tribes. It crossed the Atlas Mountains and took Fez in 1075, Tangier and Oujda in 1079, Tlemcen in 1080 and Ceuta in 1083, with Algiers, Ténès and Oran in 1082-83. He made Marrakesh, begun in 1070, his capital in place of Aghmat. In 1085 Alfonso VI captured Toledo and took tribute from Muslim princes, and al-Mu'tamid of Seville called on Yusuf, saying he would rather be a camel-driver in Africa than a swineherd in Castile.

On 23 October 1086 Yusuf, with about 15,000 men and 10,000 Andalusian fighters, won the Battle of Sagrajas, but the death of his heir sent him back to Africa. When he returned in 1090 he failed to take Toledo, and he judged the taifa kings lax and exiled the emirs of Granada and Málaga to Aghmat, followed by al-Mu'tamid a year later. All the Muslim lands of the peninsula but Zaragoza came under him. His forces defeated Alfonso at Consuegra in 1097, and after El Cid's death in 1099 a seven-month siege led by Mazdali ibn Tilankan gave him Valencia.

Medieval writers described Yusuf as wise and shrewd, suited to the Sahara and uninterested in Andalusian court pomp. He spoke Arabic poorly. He died in 1106 and his son Ali ibn Yusuf succeeded him. Andalusian revolt began from Córdoba about 1119, Christian pressure grew in the north and the Almohads, from about 1120, engulfed the south, so that his territories broke up under his successors Ibrahim ibn Tashfin and Ishaq ibn Ali, the last Almoravid rulers.
yuzhno-sakhalinsk: Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, whose name means South Sakhalin City, lies on the island of Sakhalin in the Russian Far East, north of Japan, and is the administrative centre of Sakhalin Oblast. It is the hub of the island's road and rail network, with roads running south to Korsakov and west to Kholmsk. The city is united with ten rural localities as a city of oblast significance.

The city began as a small settlement called Vladimirovka, founded by convicts in 1882. The Treaty of Portsmouth of 1905, which ended the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, awarded the southern half of Sakhalin to Japan. The settlement was renamed Toyohara, meaning bountiful plain, and became the capital of the Japanese Karafuto Prefecture, a status it kept until 1946.

During the Soviet–Japanese War, in the Second World War, Soviet troops recaptured the city. It passed to the Soviet Union and was renamed Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, and it received town status in 1946. One of the few remaining Japanese buildings now houses the local museum. It was completed in 1937 to a design by the architect Yoshio Kaizuka in the Emperor's Crown Style.

The population was 181,587 at the 2021 census, making it the largest city on the island. Gas and oil extraction and processing are among the main industries of Sakhalin, and the oil companies ExxonMobil and Shell have kept their headquarters and residential complexes in the city, although most of the investment was in the north of the island. The island's narrow-gauge railways were converted to Russian broad gauge in August 2019. Higher education includes Sakhalin State University, and the Gorny Vozdukh ski resort on Mount Bolshevik is qualified for international competitions.
